summary_plain: 180 Hebrew root words drawn directly from ACR Search's Hebrew Roots tool, each with its Paleo-Hebrew script, modern Hebrew spelling, transliteration, root letters, and full meaning — reproduced here verbatim, not summarized.

key_terms.definition: The name of the Creator. Four consonants, the Tetragrammaton. Appears 6,828 times in the Hebrew Bible. Present in the 1QIsa-a Great Isaiah Scroll and throughout the Dead Sea Scrolls. Not a title — the personal name.
Wrestled with El. Name given to Yaakov in Bereshit 32:29. Refers to the people of the covenant. Attested across DSS texts including 1QIsa-a and 4QDeut.

City of peace, or foundation of peace. Capital city of the covenant people — the stronghold of Tziyon that Dawid took and called the city of Dawid (Shmuel Bet 5:7), the city YHWH chose to put His name and desired for His dwelling place (Melakhim Bet 21:4; Tehillim 132:13). YHWH loves the gates of Tziyon (Tehillim 87:2); it is the joy of all the earth, the city of the great King (Tehillim 48:2), and out of it goes the Torah (Yeshayahu 2:3). Pray for the peace of Yerushalayim (Tehillim 122:6); if I forget you, O Yerushalayim, let my right hand forget its skill (Tehillim 137:5).
Dual form suggesting two regions (Upper and Lower). Place of bondage referenced in Devarim 28:68 and the Exodus narrative throughout the DSS.
Dedicated, initiated. Seventh from Adam. Taken by YHWH without dying (Bereshit 5:24). Author of 1 Enoch, one of the most-copied texts at Qumran. DSS fragments: 4Q201-212.

Covenant, binding agreement. Central term of the entire DSS corpus. Used in Bereshit 15 (covenant with Avraham), Devarim 28-30 (blessings and curses), and throughout the Damascus Document and Community Rule.
Teaching, instruction. From the root meaning to shoot or direct. The five books of Moshe. Called Orit in Ge'ez. DSS texts treat Torah as the binding covenant document — not as rabbinic law.
Commandment, directive. From the root to command. The specific instructions of YHWH. The DSS and Orit treat each commandment as an element of the covenant relationship, not a religious ritual.

Rest, cessation. From the root to stop. The seventh day, sanctified at creation (Bereshit 2:2-3). The DSS 364-day solar calendar keeps Shabbat on a fixed day every week without drift. The covenant record sets the specific Shabbat laws directly (Shemot 20:8-11; 35:3; 16:29; Amos 8:5; Yirmeyahu 17:21-22).

Righteousness, justice, rightness. One of the core covenant virtues, and YHWH's own character: "For YHWH is righteous — he loves righteous deeds — the upright shall behold his face" (Tehillim 11:7); "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne" (Tehillim 89:14). The coming Davidic king carries it as his very name: "this is the name by which he will be called: YHWH Is Our Righteousness" (Yirmeyahu 23:6). Found throughout Tehillim and the Prophets in DSS form.

Judgment, justice, ordinance, legal ruling. Paired with tzedek throughout the Prophets. The covenant record sets mishpat as YHWH's own judgment: He judges the world in righteousness and the peoples with uprightness (Tehillim 9:8; 96:13; 98:9); He gathers the nations to the Valley of Yehoshafat to enter into judgment with them (Yoel 3:2,12); He draws near for judgment as a swift witness against the wicked (Malakhi 3:5); and He brings every deed into judgment, with every secret thing (Kohelet 12:14). Also means legal case or custom.
Covenant loyalty, lovingkindness, steadfast love. Often translated mercy. Describes YHWH's faithfulness to the covenant. Not mere emotion but relational obligation. Central in Tehillim and Hoshea.
Truth, faithfulness, reliability. Related to amen. Describes both factual truth and covenantal trustworthiness. Often paired with chesed in Tehillim and the Prophets.
Blessing, gift of increase. The covenant blessings of Devarim 28:1-14 are conditional on obedience. The root barak also means to kneel, suggesting reverence in receiving.

Curse, diminishment. The covenant curses of Devarim 28:15-68 follow disobedience. The DSS 4QDeut fragments attest the curse passage. Verse 68 describes return to Egypt by ships — interpreted in DSS context as the transatlantic slave trade by some scholars.

Redemption, buying back. The go'el is the kinsman-redeemer who restores what was lost. Used of YHWH redeeming Yisrael from Egypt and referenced in 11Q13 Melchizedek scroll for the final jubilee redemption.
Return, turning back. From the verb shuv, to return. Repentance in DSS/Orit is a physical return to covenant obedience — returning to YHWH's commandments — not only an inner spiritual state.

Holiness, separateness, set-apartness. What belongs to YHWH. Vayikra 19:2: You shall be holy, for I YHWH your Creator am holy. Yeshayahu 6:3 shows the holy ones in the heavenly sanctuary proclaiming Holy, holy, holy is YHWH of hosts. Used in the Shema-connected texts.

Praise, shine, be radiant. The basis of HalleluYah (Praise YHWH). The Psalms/Tehillim use this root throughout. 11QPs (Cave 11 Psalms Scroll) contains halleluyah psalms in a different order from the Masoretic text.

Praise YHWH. A direct command form of hallel joined with Yah, the short form of YHWH's name. Appears throughout Tehillim (Psalms) in DSS form. Not a generic exclamation — an instruction to praise the Creator by name.

Prayer, supplication, intercession. The covenant record carries it directly — five Tehillim are titled tefillah, including Tehillim 90 "A tefillah of Moshe" and Tehillim 86 "A tefillah of David." The root palal means to judge or intervene, suggesting prayer as seeking YHWH's intervention.

Offering, that which is brought near. From karav, to draw near. The covenant record details the proper offerings (Vayikra 1-7; Bamidbar 28-29). The root expresses approach to YHWH through the act of bringing an offering.
Covering, atonement, ransom. Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement. The root kfr means to cover or wipe clean. Vayikra 16 sets the Day of Atonement rite in the covenant record.

Hear, listen, obey. The command that opens Devarim 6:4: Shema Yisrael YHWH Eloheinu YHWH Echad. The Nash Papyrus (2nd century BCE) is the oldest known manuscript of this text. In Hebrew, hearing implies obeying.

Wind, breath, spirit. In Bereshit 1:2 the ruach of YHWH moves over the face of the waters. In DSS texts the ruach is the animating force of life and the vehicle of prophetic revelation. Not a separate divine person in the DSS framework.
Light. First creation in Bereshit 1:3. Tehillim 119:105 names the word of YHWH a lamp to the feet and an or (light) to the path. Also the name of revelation — Torah is or for the path.

Darkness. Present before creation (Bereshit 1:2). In the late sectarian 1QS/1QM (later manipulated additions) a personified “Belial” was said to rule the sons of darkness. In the primary Orit, darkness is the pre-creation state and moral corruption, not a demon-king. Also used of moral corruption.

Heavens, sky. Dual form in Hebrew. Created on day two in Bereshit 1:6-8. 1 Enoch chapters 17-36 describe Enoch's tour of the heavens. Not described in DSS texts as a post-death dwelling for humans — YHWH's domain.
Earth, land, ground. Created in Bereshit 1:1. Also specifically the Land promised in the covenant. The DSS texts use eretz for both the planet and the specific covenant land.

Water. Dual or plural form, always plural in Hebrew. Present at creation (Bereshit 1:2). The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) and 1 Enoch both describe the primordial waters. Also used for Torah as living water.

Fire. YHWH appears in fire at Sinai (Shemot 19:18) and to Moshe in the burning bush. 1 Enoch 14:8-23 describes the heavenly throne as fire. The pit of fire in 1 Enoch 10:13 is the prison of the Watchers.

Soul, living being, self. In Bereshit 2:7 YHWH breathes into Adam and he becomes a living nefesh. In 1 Enoch 22 the nefesh of the dead wait at rest in four chambers in Sheol — not in heaven. Death is real: the dead rest in Sheol awaiting the judgment, not an immediate ascent — yet they are not extinguished, for Shmuel was roused from that rest and spoke to Sha'ul (1 Shemuel 28:15).

Name, reputation, memorial. Also the name of Noah's son Shem (ancestor of Semitic peoples). YHWH's name is holy and set apart. The suppression of YHWH's name in Greek translations (replaced by Kyrios/Lord) is documented from 200 BCE onward.
Word, thing, matter. YHWH's davar goes forth and accomplishes its purpose (Yeshayahu 55:11). The Ten Commandments are the ten Devarim (words/things). Torah as the spoken-then-written word of YHWH.

Wisdom. Central virtue of Mishlei (Proverbs) and DSS wisdom texts. 4QInstruction is the largest DSS wisdom text, teaching practical daily life grounded in the raz nihyeh (mystery of existence). Wisdom is relational knowledge of YHWH's ways, not mere intelligence.

Knowledge, intimate knowing. From the verb yada, to know deeply. In Bereshit 2:17 the tree of knowledge of good and evil. The DSS 4QInstruction uses raz nihyeh (mystery of existence) as the ultimate object of daat.

Mystery, secret. An Aramaic loanword appearing throughout DSS texts. 4QInstruction uses raz nihyeh (the mystery of what is to come/the mystery of existence) as its central concept — the hidden structure of reality that the wise one studies to understand daily life.

Together, community, unity. The name the Qumran covenant community used for itself, drawn straight from the covenant record — Devarim 33:5 sets the tribes of Israel yachad (together) under YHWH as King, and Tehillim 133:1 blesses brothers who dwell together (gam yachad). Emphasizes communal covenant renewal, separation from outsiders, and collective obedience.

Lot, destiny, portion. In the covenant record the lot is cast, but its every decision is from YHWH (Mishlei 16:33): the land was divided among the tribes by lot (Bamidbar 26:55), and the two goats of Yom Kippur were set by lot, one for YHWH and one for Azazel (Vayikra 16:8). Each person's lot is set before them — life and light, or death and darkness (Devarim 30:19): the path of the righteous is the light of dawn, shining brighter and brighter (Mishlei 4:18; Tehillim 97:11), while the way of the wicked is deep darkness (Mishlei 4:19). YHWH Himself holds a person's portion and lot (Tehillim 16:5).

Watcher, holy one. The angelic beings who descended to earth in 1 Enoch 6-11 and the Book of Giants (4Q203). 200 Watchers led by Shemihaza descended on Mount Hermon. The name means one who watches or stays awake. Their fall introduces evil into the world.

Worthlessness, without profit (beli + ya'al). In the pre-exilic Hebrew Orit it is an abstract adjective for human lawbreakers and traitors (Devarim 13:13, Shoftim 19:22, 1 Shemuel 1:16). Its personification into a cosmic prince of darkness is a late Second Temple sectarian development (1QS, CD, 1QM) — later manipulated additions, not covenant text. Distinct from HaSatan. The Damascus Document warns against the three nets of Belial: fornication, wealth, and defilement of the sanctuary.

Messenger, angel. From the root meaning work/task. A malach is a sent being with an assigned office, never an independent deity. The covenant record names them and their functions. Mikha'el is the chief prince and war-guardian of the covenant people: Daniyel 10:13, "Mikha'el, one of the chief princes, came to help me"; 12:1, "Mikha'el, the great prince who has charge of your people... your people shall be delivered." Gavri'el is the interpreter of visions: Daniyel 8:16, "Gavri'el, make this man understand the vision." The commander of the army of YHWH stands over His host (Yehoshua 5:14). One angel is sent to guard the way (Shemot 23:20) and to guard the covenant people in all their ways (Tehillim 91:11). Others execute judgment: the destroyer at Passover (Shemot 12:23) and the angel who struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of Assyria in a single night (Melakhim Bet 19:35). The cherubim guard the holy with a flaming sword (Bereshit 3:24); the serafim attend the throne and cry Holy, holy, holy (Yeshayahu 6:2-3). The faithful host do his word, obeying the voice of his word (Tehillim 103:20), are made winds and flaming fire (Tehillim 104:4), and praise Him as beings He created at His command (Tehillim 148:2,5). The Watchers transgressed their appointed boundary and did what they wanted, and were bound for judgment (Book of the Watchers, 1 Chanokh). Obedient or fallen, every malach is a created being with a specific task, never an independent deity.
Jubilee, ram's horn, year of release. Every 50th year in Vayikra 25. 11QMelchizedek uses jubilee timing for the final redemption.

Passover, to pass over. The night YHWH passed over the houses marked with blood in Egypt (Shemot 12). The Qumran calendar places Pesach on different dates from the Pharisaic calendar due to the 364-day solar year. The DSS community observed it as a covenant renewal.

Temple, palace, hall. The inner hall of the sanctuary. The covenant record gives YHWH's own instructions for the sanctuary — the Mishkan pattern shown to Moshe (Shemot 25-31), the temple Shlomo built (Melakhim Aleph 6-7), and the visionary temple of Yechezkel 40-48. The Qumran community treated their own assembly as a living substitute for the defiled Jerusalem temple.

Ark, chest, box. The Ark of the Covenant (Aron HaBrit) housed the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. The covenant record places it last in the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place of Shlomo's temple (Melakhim Aleph 8:6); Yirmeyahu declared it would no longer be spoken of, remembered, or made again (Yirmeyahu 3:16). It has not been seen since the Babylonian destruction.

Sign, mark, token. The rainbow is the ot of the Noachide covenant (Bereshit 9:12). Tzitzit (fringes) are an ot of the covenant (Bamidbar 15:39). The Shabbat is an ot between YHWH and Yisrael forever (Shemot 31:13). Also: the first letter, Aleph, is itself named ot.

Remembrance, memorial. YHWH commands Israel to remember the Exodus, the Sabbath, and the covenant. The root zakhar means to remember and to act on what is remembered. In DSS texts, forgetting the covenant is the root of the curse of Devarim 28.

Exile, captivity, dispersal. The covenant curses of Devarim 28 culminate in exile. The DSS community understood themselves as living in a form of exile. The Damascus Document (CD) opens describing the exile of the covenant people and their flight to Damascus.

To return, turn back. The action word of repentance. In Devarim 30:2 YHWH promises restoration when the people shuv (return) to him with all their heart. DSS texts treat shuv as the central act of covenant renewal.

Heart, mind, inner person. In ancient Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of reason and will, not just emotion. Shema Yisrael requires love with all your heart (Devarim 6:5). Tehillim 24:3-4 sets who may ascend the mountain of YHWH — the one with clean hands and a pure heart (bar levav); Devarim 10:16 commands to circumcise the foreskin of the heart.

Living being, person, appetite, life. Devarim 6:5 commands love with all your nefesh. In 1 Enoch 22 the nefesh of the righteous and wicked wait in separate chambers in Sheol. Not an immortal essence — the nefesh that sins dies (Yehezkel 18:20).

Hand, power, authority. Shemot 13:9 says the commandments are a sign on your hand. Tzitzit cords are tied on the hands. Also used metaphorically for YHWH's power — the hand of YHWH. The letter Yod (the smallest Hebrew letter) is the first letter of YHWH.

Eye, spring of water, appearance. Devarim 6:8 says the commandments are frontlets between your eyes. Also the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (𐤏). A spring or source of water shares this name — what the eye and a spring have in common is they both reveal what is beneath.

Bread, food, sustenance. Shemot 16 — the manna in the wilderness. Shemot 24:11 records the covenant meal — after the covenant was sealed, the elders ate and drank before YHWH; Bereshit 14:18 shows Malki-Tzedek, priest of the Most High, bringing out bread and wine. The bread of presence (lechem ha-panim) was set before YHWH in the sanctuary continuously.

Blood. Life is in the blood (Vayikra 17:11). Covenant ratification involved blood (Shemot 24:8). The prohibition on consuming blood is found throughout Vayikra and in the Damascus Document (CD 12:13). The Devarim 28:68 slave trade involved the shedding of blood.

Life, living. Always plural in Hebrew. YHWH is El Chayyim, the living Creator. The Torah is eitz chayyim (tree of life) to those who hold it. Devarim 30:19-20 sets YHWH as the source of the covenant people's life — "choose life... for He is your life and the length of your days."

Death. The nefesh that sins dies (Yehezkel 18:20). Death is real: the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to the Creator who gave it (Kohelet 12:7). It is no immediate passage to heaven — the dead are in Sheol below, from which Shmuel was brought up and spoke to Sha'ul, knowing him and foretelling that tomorrow he and his sons would be with him (1 Shemuel 28:15,19). YHWH will swallow up death forever and wipe away every tear (Yeshayahu 25:8). Moshe died and was buried by YHWH (Devarim 34:6).

Peace, wholeness, completeness. Not just absence of conflict but total flourishing. The covenant blessings include shalom. Used as a greeting in the DSS texts. The root shalem means to be complete or to make payment — shalom is the state of everything being in right order.

Sin, missing the mark. From the root meaning to miss a target. Shemot 34:7 and Vayikra 16:21 name the three categories together — chet (sin), pesha (rebellion), and avon (iniquity). Distinct from pesha (rebellion/transgression) and avon (iniquity/twisted action). Covenant violation in DSS is measured against specific commandments.

Servant, slave, worker. Also worshiper — to serve and to worship share the same root (avad). The covenant people are described as servants of YHWH. In Devarim 28:68 the curse warns of being sold as servants — the slave trade passage. Avad also means to work the land.

Shepherd, herdsman. YHWH is described as shepherd in Tehillim 23. Moshe, David, and the patriarchs were shepherds. The DSS Damascus Document uses shepherd imagery for community leaders. The root r'h also means to see and to pasture — a shepherd sees and feeds.

Prophet, spokesperson. One called to speak YHWH's words to the people. Devarim 13:1-5 gives the test: a prophet who teaches violation of Torah is false regardless of signs. The DSS Pesher texts interpret classical prophecy as being fulfilled in their own era.

Priest. From the tribe of Levi, specifically Aaronite descent. The Qumran community was led by priests — the Sons of Zadok (kohanim). The covenant record details the priestly duties — the consecration of Aharon and his sons, their garments, and their charge (Shemot 28-29; Vayikra 8-10; Bamidbar 18).

King, ruler. YHWH alone is King: "I am YHWH, your Holy One, the Creator of Yisra'EL, your King" (Yeshayahu 43:15); "YHWH is our judge, YHWH is our lawgiver, YHWH is our king — he will save us" (Yeshayahu 33:22); "YHWH is King forever and ever" (Tehillim 10:16); "YHWH reigns — he is robed in majesty" (Tehillim 93:1). The kingdom is His: "For kingship belongs to YHWH, and he rules over the nations" (Tehillim 22:28); "Yours is the kingdom, O YHWH, and you are exalted as head above all" (Divrei HaYamim Aleph 29:11). In 1 Samuel 8 the people's demand for a human king was a rejection of YHWH's kingship — "when YHWH your Creator was your king" (1 Shemuel 12:12). The covenant record foretells the coming Davidic king under YHWH: "There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Yishai" (Yeshayahu 11:1); "I will raise up for Dawid a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king" (Yirmeyahu 23:5); "My servant Dawid shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd" (Yechezkel 34:23-24). And YHWH shuts the door on every rival king, savior, or deity — including the Roman-era invented Yeshua figure set up as king and god: "the King of Yisra'EL and his Redeemer, YHWH of hosts: I am the first and I am the last — besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 44:6); "I, I am YHWH, and besides me there is no savior" (Yeshayahu 43:11); "I am YHWH, and there is no other. Besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 45:5); "Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth. For I am Creator, and there is no other" (Yeshayahu 45:22); "you know no Creator but me, and besides me there is no savior" (Hoshea 13:4); "YHWH is The Creator — there is no other besides him" (Devarim 4:35). No man is that deity: "The Creator is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind" (Bamidbar 23:19). To crown any other is idolatry: "You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I YHWH your Creator am a jealous Creator" (Shemot 20:5); "I am YHWH — that is my name. My glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols" (Yeshayahu 42:8); "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands" (Tehillim 115:4).

Father. Also the letter Aleph-Bet (Aleph + Bet = father). YHWH is described as father of Yisrael (Devarim 32:6). The patriarchs (avot) are Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. The word av is one of the first words a child learns in Hebrew.

Mother. The root em also means people/nation. Honoring father and mother (av ve'em) is the fifth commandment (Shemot 20:12). Also related to emet (truth) — the mother as the foundation of the household. The word am (people) may derive from the same root.

Son, child, member of a group. Bereshit opens with YHWH creating the heavens and earth and the human family begins. Ben can also mean a member of a category — b'nei Yisrael (sons of Israel = the Israelite people), b'nei Elohim (sons of God = angels in 1 Enoch 6).

Daughter. Feminine form of ben. Bat Yisrael (daughter of Israel) — a term for the covenant women. The daughters of the Yachad community at Qumran are mentioned in the Damascus Document. Also used metaphorically — Bat Tzion (daughter of Zion) for Jerusalem.

House, household, temple. Beit YHWH is the house of YHWH — the sanctuary. Beit Yisrael is the house of Israel. The covenant is made with households, not just individuals. The letter Bet (𐤁) means house — it is the second letter and the first letter of Bereshit (In the beginning).

Day. In the DSS 364-day solar calendar, days begin at sunrise (not sunset as in rabbinic tradition). Yom Kippur, Yom HaBikkurim and other holy days fall on fixed days of the week in the DSS calendar, never drifting to different weekdays as in the lunar calendar.

Night. In Bereshit 1 evening and morning mark each creation day. The Shabbat in DSS runs sunrise to sunrise, making night part of the new day — distinct from the rabbinic sunset-to-sunset tradition. 1 Enoch describes the angel of night keeping watch.
Year, repetition. The DSS 364-day solar year has exactly 52 weeks, keeping every festival on the same day of the week every year. The root shanah also means to repeat or to change.

Month, new thing. Related to chadash (new). In the DSS 364-day calendar, each month has 30 days and seasons are separated by an intercalary day (91 days per quarter). This differs from the lunar calendar which adds days to match the moon cycle.

Mountain. Har Sinai (Mount Sinai) where Torah was given. Har Hermon where the Watchers descended in 1 Enoch 6:6. Har HaBayit (Temple Mount) in Jerusalem. Mountains in DSS texts are both geographical and cosmic — boundary points between earth and heaven.

Wilderness, desert, place of speaking. The root is davar (word). The wilderness is where YHWH speaks. The Yachad community went to the wilderness of Judea specifically (citing Yeshayahu 40:3: prepare the way of YHWH in the wilderness).

Sea, west. The great bodies of water in the Hebrew world. The Sea of Reeds (Yam Suph) in the Exodus. 1 Enoch 17-19 describes the cosmic sea at the edge of the earth. Yam also means west in Hebrew since the Mediterranean Sea was to the west of the land.

Scroll, book, document, letter. From the root safar, to count/number/tell. The Dead Sea Scrolls are called sifrei Qumran in Hebrew. The Sefer Torah is the scroll of Torah. Also sofer (scribe) comes from the same root — one who records.

War, battle. In the covenant record the war belongs to YHWH: YHWH is a warrior — YHWH is His name (Shemot 15:3). When you go out to war against an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid, for YHWH your Creator is with you (Devarim 20:1), He it is who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory (Devarim 20:4). He is YHWH strong and mighty, YHWH mighty in battle (Tehillim 24:8). The root lechem (bread) shares the same root — both involve struggle for survival.

Salvation, deliverance, rescue. YHWH is described as yeshuah throughout Tehillim. The name Yeshua, the personal name the NT assigns to its invented figure, comes from this root and means YHWH saves. In DSS/Orit context, salvation is covenant restoration — the physical return of the people to their land and covenant.

Eternal, age, long duration, hidden. Brit olam is an eternal covenant. YHWH's covenant with Avraham is l'olam va'ed — forever and ever. The root also means hidden or concealed, suggesting that eternity is beyond what can be fully seen from the present moment.

Understanding, discernment, between-ness. From the preposition bein (between) — understanding is the ability to distinguish between things. One of the three qualities in Mishlei 8 alongside wisdom and knowledge. The DSS Maskil (teaching leader) was required to demonstrate binah.

Fear, awe, reverence. Tehillim 111:10 and Mishlei 1:7 both state: the fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom. In DSS usage yirat YHWH is not terror but the deep recognition of YHWH's reality and authority that shapes all decisions.

Keep, guard, watch, observe. Shomer Shabbat — keeper of the Sabbath. The covenant people are commanded to shamar (keep) the commandments (Devarim 6:17). In DSS the Maskil keeps/guards the community's covenant standards. Also a watchman on the city wall.

Walk, go, live according to. Halakhah (Jewish law) comes from this root — the way one walks. The DSS community spoke of walking in the perfect way. Micah 6:8: walk humbly with your Creator. Enoch walked (halakh) with YHWH — the same verb used for his unique relationship.

River, stream. The four rivers of Eden (Bereshit 2:10-14). The River Euphrates marks the boundary of the covenant land. 1 Enoch 17-19 describes Enoch crossing cosmic rivers of fire and water. Nahar also means to flow or to shine.

Oil, fat, richness. The anointing oil (shemen mishchah) was used to consecrate the priests and sanctuary. The menorah burned pure olive oil. The word mashiach (anointed one/Messiah) comes from the related verb. The covenant blessings include abundance of oil.

Wine. Bamidbar 28:14 sets the yayin (wine) drink offering poured to YHWH in the sanctuary, and Bereshit 14:18 shows Malki-Tzedek, priest of the Most High, bringing out bread and wine. Also the third item in the covenant blessing list of grain, oil, and wine (Devarim 11:14). The DSS community maintained strict rules about who could participate in the communal wine-blessing ceremony.

Honey, date syrup. The land flowing with milk and honey (chalav u'dvash) — the covenant land described throughout Torah. The DSS calendar festivals include first-fruit offerings of wine, oil, wheat, and honey. Some scholars identify dvash here as date syrup rather than bee honey.

People, nation, kinship group. Am Yisrael (the people of Israel). YHWH says: you will be my am and I will be your Elohim (covenant formula throughout the prophets). Devarim 29:9-14 sets who enters the am — all Israel standing before YHWH to enter the covenant, down to the stranger in the camp.

Assembly, congregation, gathering. The kahal of Yisrael is the covenant assembly. The DSS texts have detailed rules about who may enter the kahal — those with physical defects, the ritually impure, or the wicked are excluded. Also the source of the English word ecclesiastical.

Lamb, young sheep or goat. The Pesach offering is a seh (Shemot 12:3). The daily tamid offering is also a seh. The covenant record details the requirements for sacrificial animals — a male without blemish (Shemot 12:5; Vayikra 22:19-25). The lamb represents innocence and the substitutionary nature of the korban system.

Tabernacle, dwelling place. From the root shakhon, to dwell. YHWH's mishkan traveled with Yisrael in the wilderness. The covenant record describes YHWH's mishkan in great detail — the pattern shown to Moshe and its construction (Shemot 25-31; 35-40), until the glory of YHWH filled it (Shemot 40:34). The root also gives us shekhinah — the divine presence that dwells among the people.

Remember, recall, mention. YHWH commands Yisrael to remember the Exodus, the Sabbath, and the covenant. In DSS thought, forgetting the covenant (shikach) is the act that leads to the curses of Devarim 28. The root also means male — perhaps the one who carries the memory forward.

Know, experience, be intimate with. YHWH knows (yada) each person fully. Moshe was known face to face by YHWH (Devarim 34:10). The DSS text of Hoshea 4:6 uses yada for the people's destruction from lack of knowledge — not intellectual knowledge but relational covenant knowledge.

See, look, perceive. YHWH sees everything — Bereshit 16:13, El Roi (the El who sees me). The root appears in roeh (seer/prophet — one who sees). Also in Yerushalayim — city of the vision. The DSS texts describe prophets as those who have seen the divine council.

Hear, listen, obey. The opening word of the Shema. In Hebrew, hearing implies responding and obeying. The DSS Damascus Document condemns those who hear the Torah but do not obey it. The root shama gives us shomea (listener) and mishma'at (obedience/jurisdiction).

Creation, what is created. From bara (to create out of nothing — an act only YHWH performs). Bereshit 1:1 — In the beginning YHWH created (bara) the heavens and the earth. The 1QapGen (Genesis Apocryphon) retells creation with additional detail. Human beings form but do not bara.

Redemption, release from obligation. The go'el (kinsman-redeemer) had legal duty to redeem land, free family members from slavery, and avenge blood. YHWH acts as the go'el of Yisrael (Yeshayahu 41:14). The 11Q13 Melchizedek text describes the final redemption using this framework.

Praise, song of praise, glory. The plural tehillim gives us the name of the Book of Psalms. The 11QPs scroll from Cave 11 contains 41 psalms not found in the canonical psalter plus the Great Psalms Scroll arrangement. Tehillim were sung in the DSS communal worship.

The short form of YHWH's name. Used at the end of HalleluYah and many Hebrew personal names (EliYah, YeshiYahu, NechamYah). Present in the DSS texts alongside the full Tetragrammaton. Some DSS scribes wrote Yah in Paleo-Hebrew script even within otherwise square-script texts.

All, every, whole. Shema Yisrael: love YHWH with all (kol) your heart, all your soul, all your strength. Kol Yisrael — all Israel. In DSS the covenant applies to kol — the whole community. Also means voice when voweled differently (kol YHWH — the voice of YHWH).

New, renewed. Brit chadashah — new/renewed covenant (Yirmeyahu 31:31). In DSS interpretation this new covenant was the one the Qumran community believed they were living. The root also gives chodesh (month/new moon). New in Hebrew implies renewal of something established, not replacement.

Ancient, primordial, from the east. The Ancient of Days (Attiq Yomin) in Daniyel 7:9 is a DSS-era text describing YHWH on the throne. The DSS interest in primordial history — creation, Watchers, Enoch — reflects a concern with qadmon times as the source of understanding.

God is my judge — from Dan (judge) and El (God). The Book of Daniel was one of the most copied texts at Qumran: 8 manuscripts found across multiple caves. The DSS community read Daniel's 70-weeks prophecy (Daniel 9) as describing their own era. Daniel is written in both Hebrew and Aramaic, making it unique among the prophetic books.

Rest, comfort, relief. YHWH chose Noach because he was righteous in his generation (Bereshit 6:9). The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) from Cave 1 retells the Noach story in vivid detail including his miraculous birth. The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch) gives Noach his own birth narrative and presents him as a precursor to the coming Messianic figure.

Initiated, dedicated. Chanoch walked with Elohim and was taken without dying (Bereshit 5:24). The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch) is the most extensively attested non-biblical text at Qumran — 7 Aramaic manuscript fragments found across the caves. Chanoch is the central visionary of DSS cosmology, the 364-day solar calendar, and angelology. No figure outside Torah is more important to the DSS worldview.

Drawn from water — named by Pharaoh's daughter who drew him from the Nile (Shemot 2:10). The lawgiver of Yisrael; YHWH spoke to him face to face (Devarim 34:10). The DSS community saw themselves as re-living the Moshe wilderness period. The Temple Scroll (11QT) rewrites Torah in the first person as if spoken by YHWH directly to Moshe, replacing "he" with "I" throughout.

Father of many nations — from av hamon goyim (Bereshit 17:5). Originally Avram (exalted father) until YHWH changed his name at the covenant of circumcision. The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) retells Avraham's journeys in narrative.

He laughs, laughter. Named because Sarah laughed when told she would bear a son in old age (Bereshit 18:12). The Akedah — the binding of Yitzchak (Bereshit 22) — is central to DSS covenant theology. The Jubilees text retells the Akedah with the figure of Mastema (the accuser) prompting the test of Avraham, parallel to the Job prologue. Yitzchak is the son of promise through whom the covenant line continues.

He grasps the heel, supplanter. Born holding Esau's heel (Bereshit 25:26). YHWH renamed him Yisrael — one who wrestles with God (Bereshit 32:28). Patriarch of the 12 tribes. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs (related to DSS literature) presents the deathbed speeches of each of Yaakov's sons. The Damascus Document begins its history of the covenant with the community as the new house of Yaakov.

My God is YHWH. The prophet who confronted the prophets of Baal at Carmel (1 Kings 18) and was taken up in a whirlwind without dying (2 Kings 2:11) — like Chanoch. Malachi 4:5 promises Eliyahu will return before the great Day of YHWH. The DSS community expected an Elijah-like forerunner alongside the Davidic Messiah — a priestly and a royal figure together.

Beloved, kinsman. King of Yisrael and author of much of Tehillim (Psalms). The DSS Messianic expectation centers on a Davidic Messiah (Mashiach ben David) who would restore the kingdom. The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs) from Cave 11 attributes 3,600 psalms to David. The Davidic covenant stands in the covenant record itself: "I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:12); "your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me" (2 Samuel 7:16). That Mashiach is a human king and YHWH's servant — never a deity: "my servant Dawid shall be prince among them. I am YHWH" (Yechezkel 34:24); YHWH's Anointed, under YHWH, not YHWH (Tehillim 2:2). YHWH is one and is worshipped alone: "Hear, O Yisra'EL: YHWH our Creator, YHWH is one" (Devarim 6:4); "You shall have no other deities before me" (Shemot 20:3); "You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I YHWH your Creator am a jealous Creator" (Shemot 20:5). No man is that god: "The Creator is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man" (Bamidbar 23:19); "besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 44:6). The NT's invented figure was built to break this commandment: it sets the manufactured Yeshua up as a mandatory mediator-deity and puts in his mouth "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6) — forcing a fabricated god between the people and YHWH. That is idolatry by definition — another deity set before YHWH — in flat violation of "YHWH is one" and "You shall have no other deities before me." The covenant record installs no mediator and crowns no god beside YHWH; the gateway-Yeshua is the counterfeit the commandment forecloses.

Peace, from shalom. Son of David who built the First Temple in Jerusalem. The DSS community was deeply critical of the Jerusalem Temple establishment — seeing the Hasmonean high priests as illegitimate replacements of the Zadokite line. The Copper Scroll (3Q15) may reference Temple treasures traceable to the era of Shlomo's Temple. Songs of Songs (Shir HaShirim) is attributed to Shlomo and was found at Qumran.

YHWH saves, salvation of YHWH. The prophet whose book was the most copied scripture at Qumran. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) is the oldest complete biblical manuscript in existence, dated to around 125 BCE and currently housed in the Israel Museum. The DSS community read Isaiah 40:3 — prepare the way of YHWH in the wilderness — as their own mandate for going to Qumran.

YHWH exalts or YHWH throws down. The prophet who witnessed the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE. His prophecy of the new covenant (Brit Chadashah, Yirmeyahu 31:31-34) is the most cited prophetic text in the DSS. The Qumran community believed they were the people of this renewed covenant. A Letter of Jeremiah is found among the DSS (7Q2).

Human, mankind, earth-creature. From adamah (ground/earth). YHWH formed Adam from the dust of the ground (Bereshit 2:7), made in the image of the Creator: "So the Creator created man in his own image, in the image of the Creator he created him — male and female he created them" (Bereshit 1:27). At his transgression Adam was driven from the garden and returned to the dust: "you are dust, and to dust you shall return" (Bereshit 3:19); "He drove out the man, and at the east of the Garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword" (Bereshit 3:24).

My king is righteousness, or king of righteousness. The mysterious priest-king of Salem who blessed Avraham (Bereshit 14:18-20). Tehillim 110:4 declares the Messiah a priest forever after the order of Malkitzedeq. The DSS Melchizedek text (11Q13) from Cave 11 presents Malkitzedeq as a heavenly figure who will execute divine judgment in the final Yom Kippur — one of the most remarkable Messianic documents found at Qumran.

In the beginning. The first word and Hebrew name of the first book of Torah. Bereshit covers creation through the death of Yosef. Multiple copies were found at Qumran, making it among the most attested Torah books in the DSS. The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) is an Aramaic retelling of Bereshit with expanded narrative.

Names — the second book of Torah, named for its opening words "these are the names." Covers the bondage in Egypt, the ten plagues, the Exodus, the giving of Torah at Sinai, and the building of the Mishkan. Shemot is foundational to the DSS covenant theology — the community saw itself as re-living the Sinai covenant in the wilderness period.

And He called — the third book of Torah, the priestly manual. Covers sacrificial law, purity codes, festivals, and the Holiness Code (chapters 17-26). Vayikra is among the most cited Torah texts in the DSS. The Qumran community applied Levitical purity standards to their own communal life, treating the community itself as a living temple.

In the wilderness — the fourth book of Torah. Covers the 40-year wilderness wandering, the census of Yisrael, the rebellion cycles, and the approach to the promised land. Bamidbar's wilderness setting was central to the DSS community's self-understanding — citing Isaiah 40:3 and Bamidbar 9:1-14, they went to the Judean desert to prepare the way of YHWH. Bamidbar itself sets the military census — "From twenty years old and upward, all in Yisra'EL who are able to go to war" (Bamidbar 1:3) — and the camp order, each tribe under its own standard around the tent of meeting (Bamidbar 2:2).

Words — the fifth and final book of Torah. Moshe's farewell speeches to Yisrael before his death. Contains the Shema (6:4), the blessings and curses (chapters 27-30), and the covenant renewal. Devarim is the most cited Torah book in the entire DSS corpus. The DSS community saw Devarim 17:14-20 (the law of the king) as directly applicable to their rejection of Hasmonean rule.

Praises, hymns — the book of Psalms. Attributed largely to David. The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs) from Cave 11 is one of the largest DSS manuscripts and includes 41 psalms not found in the standard canon plus a prose statement crediting David with 3,600 psalms. Tehillim was the most copied book at Qumran after Isaiah and Devarim. The Hodayot (Thanksgiving Hymns) found at Qumran were composed in the style and vocabulary of Tehillim.

Proverbs, parables — attributed to Shlomo. The wisdom literature of Yisrael alongside Iyov and Kohelet. Fragments of Mishlei were found at Qumran (4QProv). The DSS community's emphasis on wisdom (Sekhel, Binah, Da'at) reflects direct engagement with Mishlei's teaching. The figure of personified Wisdom (Chokhmah) in Mishlei 8 — present at creation — is developed in the DSS Songs of the Sage (4Q510-511).

Job — the book of suffering and divine justice. An Aramaic targum (translation) of Iyov was found at Qumran (11QtgJob), making it one of the earliest known translations of any biblical text. The book's wrestling with theodicy — why the righteous suffer — was directly relevant to the DSS community who experienced exile, persecution, and the sense of YHWH's justice delayed. The heavenly council scene (Job 1-2) with the adversary parallels DSS angelology.

YHWH saves — the same root as Yeshuah (salvation). Yehoshua ben Nun led Yisrael into the land after Moshe. The book describes the conquest and allotment of Canaan. A paraphrase of Yehoshua was found at Qumran (4QJosh). The DSS community saw themselves as a new Yehoshua generation about to re-enter the land. Yehoshua's own military theology gives the battle to YHWH: the commander of the army of YHWH stood before Yehoshua (Yehoshua 5:14), and at Yericho the wall fell flat when the people shouted, for "YHWH has given you the city" (Yehoshua 6:16, 20).

El strengthens — the prophet of the Babylonian exile. His chariot vision (Merkavah, chapters 1 and 10) of the divine throne-chariot was one of the most studied texts at Qumran. Multiple Yechezkel manuscripts were found at Qumran.

Salvation, YHWH saves. The first of the Twelve Minor Prophets. Hoshea used his marriage to an unfaithful wife as a metaphor for Yisrael's covenant unfaithfulness. Fragments of a Hoshea Pesher (commentary) were found at Qumran (4QpHos), applying Hoshea's prophecies to the community's own era. Hoshea 4:6 — my people perish for lack of knowledge (da'at) — was a key proof text for the Qumran emphasis on Torah knowledge.

Burden-bearer. The shepherd-prophet of the 8th century BCE who spoke against social injustice and empty ritual. Amos closes with the covenant promise of restoration: "In that day I will raise up the booth of Dawid that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old" (Amos 9:11).

Who is like YHWH. The prophet who challenged the corrupt leadership of Jerusalem. Michah 6:8 — do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with your Creator — is the ethical summary of the covenant. Fragments of Michah were found at Qumran. Michah 5:2 (from Bethlehem a ruler will come) is cited as a Messianic text. The community valued Michah's vision of swords beaten into plowshares (4:3) as describing the post-Messianic age of peace.

Embrace or wrestler. The prophet who cried out to YHWH about violence and the rise of the Babylonians — "O YHWH, how long shall I cry for help?" (Chavakuk 1:2). YHWH answered that the vision awaits its appointed time and will not lie (Chavakuk 2:3), and that the righteous shall live by his faithfulness (Chavakuk 2:4) — a cornerstone of covenant theology. YHWH is in His holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before Him (Chavakuk 2:20). The prophet, hearing the report of YHWH, prayed, "in wrath remember mercy" (Chavakuk 3:2); and though the fig tree does not blossom, he still rejoices in YHWH (Chavakuk 3:17-18).

The Rule of the Community — the foundational constitution of the Qumran community found in Cave 1 (1QS). Details entry requirements, communal meals, discipline procedures, the two-spirit doctrine (Spirit of Truth vs. Spirit of Deceit), and the eschatological hymns. One of the first scrolls discovered in 1947. Multiple copies found across the caves, showing it was a living, edited document. Not covenant scripture — a late Second Temple sectarian rulebook not found in the authentic record, carrying no covenant authority. The 4Q258 copy preserves an earlier layer where authority sat with the general assembly; the finalized Cave 1 scroll shows scribes inserting text that handed absolute veto to the Sons of Zadok — a power grab caught on the leather.

The Damascus Covenant — also called the Damascus Document (CD). Found originally in the Cairo Geniza in 1896, then confirmed at Qumran in Caves 4, 5, and 6. Describes the founding of the community after 390 years of divine wrath following the Babylonian exile, the role of the Teacher of Righteousness, halakhic rules, and warnings against the Man of the Lie. The Damesek reference may be literal (Syria) or symbolic (Amos 5:27). Not covenant scripture — a late Second Temple sectarian rulebook not found in the authentic record, carrying no covenant authority. Its 390-year figure is a schematic self-dating the sect drew from Yechezkel 4:5 to legitimize its own founding.

The final war of the covenant — the end-times battle in which YHWH Himself goes to war for His people. YHWH will go out and fight against the nations as when He fights on a day of battle (Zecharyah 14:3); YHWH is a warrior, YHWH is His name (Shemot 15:3). He gathers all the nations down to the Valley of Yehoshafat and enters into judgment with them there (Yoel 3:2,12). The covenant people are mustered for it — numbered from twenty years old and up, all able to go to war (Bamidbar 1:3), each camped under his own standard and banner (Bamidbar 2:2), sounding the war-trumpet to be remembered before YHWH and saved from the enemy (Bamidbar 10:9). It is a war of light against darkness: though darkness covers the earth and thick darkness the peoples, YHWH arises upon His people and His glory is seen (Yeshayahu 60:1-2); the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (Yeshayahu 9:2). Its end is the kingdom of YHWH — saviors go up to Mount Tziyon and the kingdom is YHWH's (Ovadyah 1:21); YHWH will be king over all the earth, YHWH one and His name one (Zecharyah 14:9).

The Temple Scroll — the largest of the Dead Sea Scrolls (11QT, Cave 11, ~8.6 meters). Rewrites large portions of Torah in first-person voice as if YHWH is speaking directly. Covers the ideal Temple layout in elaborate detail, festival laws following the 364-day solar calendar, and the law of the king (a sectarian rewrite of Devarim 17). The scroll presents an ideal Israel that the Qumran community believed would be established in the Messianic era. Not covenant scripture — a late Second Temple sectarian forgery put in YHWH's mouth, not found in the authentic record, carrying no covenant authority.

Songs of thanksgiving — a collection of hymns. The hymns describe deliverance from the wicked, the experience of divine election, and the suffering of the righteous leader. Written in the style and language of Tehillim (Psalms). A late Second Temple sectarian hymn, not covenant scripture — a later manipulated addition to the record.

The Book of Jubilees (Mashafa Kufale / 4Q216-224) — a retelling of Bereshit through the giving of the Torah at Sinai, organized into 49 periods of 7 years each (jubilees). Written as YHWH's direct dictation to Moshe via an angel of the presence. Some fifteen Hebrew copies were recovered across five Qumran caves — more copies than many books in the received canon; the oldest (4Q216) dates by its Hasmonean script to c. 125-100 BCE. Jubilees 6:17-38 cites the 364-day solar calendar as the divinely mandated structure of time, the same calendar independently attested at 4Q208-4Q209. Complete only in the Ge'ez Orit, preserved by the Beta Israel community.

The Book of Enoch — the most extensively attested non-Torah text at Qumran in Aramaic fragments. Two sections are the pre-Corruption covenant baseline, both physically attested at Qumran: the Book of Watchers (ch. 1-36, the Watcher/Nephilim account) and the Astronomical Book (ch. 72-82, the 364-day solar calendar). The other three sections carried in the later Ge'ez collection — the Similitudes (ch. 37-71), the Book of Dreams (ch. 83-90), and the Epistle of Enoch (ch. 91-108) — are text manipulation added after the covenant record, not covenant text; the Similitudes has no fragment among the Qumran Enoch copies. Preserved in the Ge'ez (Ethiopian) Orit tradition. The DSS community treated the Watchers and Astronomical Book as authoritative scripture. Chanoch's solar calendar in the Astronomical Book is foundational to the DSS festival system.

The Copper Scroll (3Q15) — unique among the DSS in being engraved on copper sheets rather than written on parchment or papyrus. Found in Cave 3 in 1952. Lists 64 locations where enormous quantities of gold, silver, and sacred vessels are supposedly hidden across the land. Scholars debate whether this is a real treasure map (from the First or Second Temple era), a symbolic document, or an eschatological text. No treasure has been recovered from any listed site.

Interpretation, solution, commentary. The DSS Pesharim are a late sectarian device that hijacks the prophets — decoding a prophet's words as secret references to one Qumran faction's own era: its founder-legend the "Teacher of Righteousness," its enemy the "Wicked Priest," and the "Kittim." The Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab) is the fullest example; the same method was imposed on Isaiah, Nahum, Psalms, Hosea, Micah, and Zephaniah. A 1st-century-BCE factional narrative dressed as prophetic revelation. Not found in the authentic record. A later addition of manipulation texts.

The three books of Meqabyan are part of the Ethiopian Orthodox canon (Orit tradition) and are distinct from the Greek 1-4 Maccabees. They recount the faithful resistance of YHWH's people against pagan rulers and call Yisrael back to covenant faithfulness. Not found among the DSS, but preserved in Ge'ez as part of the broader Orit canon recognized by Ethiopian Christianity and Beta Israel. The Meqabyan tradition shares the DSS emphasis on righteous suffering and ultimate divine vindication.

Life-giver, mother of all living. YHWH named her Chavah because she was the mother of all the living (Bereshit 3:20). The Aramaic Levi Document and the Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) both engage with the early chapters of Bereshit where Chavah appears. In 1 Enoch tradition the corruption introduced through the Watchers is framed against the original purity of creation — Chavah represents the beginning of the human family.

Acquired, smith, spearman. First son of Adam and Chavah; killed his brother Hevel. From the root qanah (to acquire) — Chavah said "I have acquired a man with YHWH" (Bereshit 4:1). The covenant record makes Kayin the example of the stubborn heart that rejected YHWH: warned that sin crouches at the door and that he must master it (Bereshit 4:7), he refused — the stubborn, rebellious heart the prophets condemn (Yirmeyahu 5:23; Yeshayahu 46:12). 1 Enoch treats Kayin's line as the origin of violence that provoked the Flood.

Breath, vapor, vanity. Second son of Adam and Chavah; the first to offer a pleasing sacrifice and the first to die. The name Hevel (vapor) foreshadows his brief life. Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) opens with "Hevel of Hevels — all is Hevel" — using the same root for the transience of earthly life. The DSS Aramaic texts treat Hevel's murder as the first covenant blood shed on the earth, requiring justice.

Appointed, placed, foundation. Third son of Adam and Chavah, born after Hevel's murder. YHWH appointed (shat) another seed in place of Hevel (Bereshit 4:25). The righteous line from Adam runs through Shet to Noach. 1 Enoch traces Chanoch's wisdom through the Shet lineage. The DSS Aramaic Levi Document traces the priestly line through Shet. In some DSS traditions Shet is presented as a figure of restoration after the rupture of Kayin.

Man of the javelin, or his death shall bring. Son of Chanoch, grandfather of Noach; lived 969 years — the longest lifespan in Bereshit 5. Metushelach is prominent in 1 Enoch: Chanoch transmitted his heavenly visions and wisdom through Metushelach before being taken. The Book of Giants (4Q531) from Qumran mentions Metushelach as a link in the chain of antediluvian revelation. His death traditionally coincided with the year of the Flood.

Strong man, powerful. Two figures named Lemech in Bereshit — one in the line of Kayin (the violent man of Bereshit 4:23-24) and one in the line of Shet, father of Noach. The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) opens with Lemech (Noach's father) troubled by his son's miraculous birth, suspecting angelic involvement, and consulting Metushelach and then Chanoch for clarification. This scene makes Lemech one of the most vividly portrayed figures in the DSS literature.

Exalted, mountain of strength, enlightened. Brother of Moshe and Miryam; the first High Priest (Kohen Gadol) of Yisrael. The Aaronite priestly line is foundational to all Temple worship law. The DSS community — led by the Sons of Zadok, who traced their lineage through Aharon — saw themselves as the legitimate priestly heirs of the Aharon covenant. The Community Rule (1QS) gives priests (sons of Aharon) the highest communal authority.

Beloved, strong waters, exalted. Sister of Moshe and Aharon; a prophetess who led the women of Yisrael in the Song of the Sea after crossing the Yam Suph (Shemot 15:20-21). Her prophetic role and her challenge to Moshe's exclusive authority (Bamidbar 12) make her one of the most significant women in Torah. Fragments of a text about Miryam were found at Qumran (4Q365). Her name is a feminine form related to bitterness and strength — given during the hardship of Egyptian bondage.

Dog, wholehearted. One of the twelve spies sent to scout Canaan; with Yehoshua he gave a faithful report and urged entry into the land. Kalev followed YHWH wholeheartedly (Bamidbar 14:24) and was granted an inheritance in the land when the rest of his generation perished in the wilderness. His name may also be read as kol-lev (whole heart). The covenant record marks him as the one who wholly followed YHWH — he received Chevron as his inheritance "because you have wholly followed YHWH my Creator" (Yehoshua 14:9).

Bee, word-speaker. The only female Judge of Yisrael; also a prophetess. Led Yisrael to victory over Sisera and Yavin of Canaan (Shoftim 4-5). The Song of Devorah (Shoftim 5) is among the oldest poetic texts in the Hebrew Bible. Her name Devorah is related to davar (word, thing) — she was known as a speaker of YHWH's word. The DSS Qumran library had a strong prophetic tradition; female prophets like Devorah were recognized as legitimate voices in the DSS theological framework.

Heard by El, or His name is El. Prophet, judge, and kingmaker. Anointed both Shaul and David as king. Fragments of the Book of Shmuel were found at Qumran in multiple versions, including a text (4QSam-a) closer to the Greek Septuagint than the standard Hebrew, revealing that multiple textual traditions circulated simultaneously. Shmuel's warning against the monarchy (1 Samuel 8) — that a human king would oppress the people — resonated strongly with the DSS community's rejection of the Hasmonean rulers.

Asked for, requested. First king of Yisrael, from the tribe of Binyamin. The people asked for (sha'al) a king like the other nations (1 Samuel 8), and YHWH gave them Shaul. His reign is characterized by early success and later disobedience — most critically, his consultation of the medium at En Dor (1 Samuel 28). The DSS text 4QSam-a contains an older version of the Shaul narratives. Shaul's failure confirmed for the DSS community that human kingship apart from YHWH's direct governance was flawed.

Given, gift. The prophet who served at David's court. Delivered the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7) — YHWH's promise that David's line would rule forever. Confronted David after the Bat-Sheva and Uriah incident with the parable of the ewe lamb. The Natan oracle is the covenant record's own promise of the coming Davidic king: "I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:12); "your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me" (2 Samuel 7:16). That Mashiach is a human king and YHWH's servant — never a deity: "my servant Dawid shall be prince among them. I am YHWH" (Yechezkel 34:24); YHWH's Anointed, under YHWH, not YHWH (Tehillim 2:2). YHWH is one and is worshipped alone: "Hear, O Yisra'EL: YHWH our Creator, YHWH is one" (Devarim 6:4); "You shall have no other deities before me" (Shemot 20:3); "You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I YHWH your Creator am a jealous Creator" (Shemot 20:5). No man is that god: "The Creator is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man" (Bamidbar 23:19); "besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 44:6). The NT's invented figure was built to break this commandment: it sets the manufactured Yeshua up as a mandatory mediator-deity and puts in his mouth "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6) — forcing a fabricated god between the people and YHWH. That is idolatry by definition — another deity set before YHWH — in flat violation of "YHWH is one" and "You shall have no other deities before me." The covenant record installs no mediator and crowns no god beside YHWH; the gateway-Yeshua is the counterfeit the commandment forecloses. Natan is the archetype of the prophetic voice that holds the king accountable to Torah.

My El saves. The disciple and successor of Eliyahu. Received a double portion of Eliyahu's spirit (2 Kings 2:9-10). Performed more recorded miracles than any other prophet in the Hebrew Bible — healing, resurrection, multiplication of food, and military guidance. His ministry to the poor, widows, and foreigners made him a beloved figure. The DSS community's expectation of a prophetic forerunner drew on both Eliyahu and Elisha traditions. Elisha's name shares the root with Yeshuah (salvation).

Friend, companion, satisfied. Moabite woman who chose to follow her mother-in-law Naomi back to Yisrael after her husband's death. Her declaration "your people will be my people, your God my God" (Rut 1:16) is one of the most powerful covenant commitment statements in all of scripture. Through Boaz she became the great-grandmother of David. The DSS community's strict rules about who could enter the covenant assembly made Rut's full inclusion — a Moabite woman — theologically striking.

He adds, He increases — named by Rachel at his birth (Bereshit 30:24). Sold into slavery in Mitzrayim by his brothers, rose to become second to Pharaoh, and preserved the covenant family through famine (Bereshit 37-50). Ya'akov's blessing on his sons Efrayim and Menasheh split Yosef's line into two tribal allotments rather than one.

Princess, noblewoman. Avraham's wife, originally named Sarai until YHWH renamed her at the covenant of circumcision (Bereshit 17:15). Mother of Yitzchak, the son of promise born to her in old age (Bereshit 21:1-3). The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) from Cave 1 expands on Sarah's beauty and the danger it posed in Mitzrayim under Pharaoh.

Dove. Prophet sent to warn Nineveh, who fled toward Tarshish instead and was swallowed by a great fish before completing his mission (Yonah 1-2). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets (Trei Asar), attested at Qumran among the fragmentary Minor Prophets manuscripts (4QXIIa-g) that preserve the Twelve as a single continuous scroll.

YHWH comforts. Cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who returned to Yerushalayim and rebuilt its broken walls (Nechemyah 1-6). Led a covenant renewal alongside Ezra, reinstating Torah reading and Sabbath observance (Nechemyah 8-10). Like Ezra, the Nechemyah narrative reflects the post-exilic scribal tradition that shaped later Second Temple Judean life.

YHWH is God. Prophet of a locust plague and coming judgment, calling for national repentance (Yoel 1-2) and promising YHWH's spirit poured out on all flesh (Yoel 2:28-29). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g).

Servant of YHWH. Shortest book in the Hebrew Bible, a judgment oracle against Edom for its violence against Yaakov's descendants (Ovadyah 1:10-14). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g).

Comfort, consolation. Prophet who announced the fall of Nineveh and Assyria's judgment for its cruelty (Nakhum 1-3), a companion oracle to Yonah's earlier warning to the same city generations before. One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g); a dedicated Nahum Pesher (4QpNah) was also found at Qumran, applying his oracle to the community's own era.

Hidden, treasured by YHWH. Prophet during Yoshiyahu's reign, announcing the coming Day of YHWH against Yehudah and the nations, with a remnant preserved (Tzefanyah 1-3). His father is named Kushi (Tzefanyah 1:1). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g).

Festive, my feast. Post-exilic prophet who urged the returned exiles to rebuild the Second Temple, dated precisely to the second year of Darius (Khagai 1:1). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g).

YHWH remembers. Post-exilic prophet, contemporary of Khagai, whose visions of lampstands, horses, and a coming king shaped later Second Temple expectation (Zekharyah 1-14). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g).

My messenger. Final prophet of the Hebrew Bible's prophetic corpus, rebuking priestly corruption and covenant unfaithfulness, and naming an Eliyahu-like messenger to come before the great Day of YHWH (Malakhi 3:1, 4:5). One of the Twelve Minor Prophets attested in the Qumran Minor Prophets scrolls (4QXIIa-g).

Help, assistance. The priest and scribe who led a return from Babylonian exile to Yisrael (around 458 BCE) and publicly read Torah to the assembled people (Nechemiah 8). Ezra is credited with establishing the public Torah reading tradition and the standardization of the Hebrew text. The DSS community's intense focus on correct Torah interpretation (Pesher, Halakhah) reflects the post-Ezra scribal tradition. Some scholars connect the founding of the Qumran community to disputes over Torah interpretation that began in the Ezra era.

Hidden, star (from the Persian). Jewish queen of Persia who saved her people from destruction through Haman's plot. Her Hebrew name was Hadassah (myrtle). The Book of Esther is the only biblical book not found among the DSS — scholars debate whether this was accidental or intentional. Possible reasons: the book never mentions the name of YHWH, does not reference the Torah or Temple, and the feast of Purim it establishes was not part of the Qumran 364-day solar calendar.

Warrior, follower of Marduk (Babylonian name form), or the bitter crushing. Cousin and guardian of Esther; refused to bow to Haman and thereby triggered the plot against the Jewish people. His faithfulness in refusing idolatrous obeisance connects to the same theme as Daniel refusing to bow and the three young men refusing the furnace. Like Esther's book, Mordechai is absent from the DSS — but his resistance to pagan authority parallels DSS theology of fidelity to YHWH over human rulers.

Who is like El? The archangel and warrior prince of the covenant people. The covenant record names him plainly: Mikha'el, one of the chief princes, comes to fight (Daniyel 10:13); Mikha'el your prince is the only one who contends at the messenger's side (Daniyel 10:21); and Mikha'el, the great prince who has charge of your people, shall arise at the time of trouble, and your people shall be delivered (Daniyel 12:1). In 1 Enoch he is one of the four archangels who intercede before YHWH over the Watcher crisis.

Strength of El, man of God. The archangel who delivers divine messages. In Daniyel 8:16 and 9:21, Gavriel appears to explain the visions of the 2,300 evenings and mornings and the 70 weeks of years. In 1 Enoch 9:1, Gavriel is one of the four archangels who bring the cry of the earth before YHWH after the Watcher corruption. Gavriel is assigned by YHWH to destroy the children of the Watchers and is the angel of power and divine communication in the DSS angelological system.

El heals, healing of God. The archangel of healing. In 1 Enoch 10:4-7, Refa'el is commanded by YHWH to bind Azazel under the earth until the final judgment. In 1 Enoch 22, Refa'el is assigned to guard the souls of the dead. His name comes from rafa (to heal), and he is the healer among the archangels. The DSS Book of Tobit (fragments found at Qumran) features Refa'el as a central character who accompanies Tobias on his journey and heals his father's blindness.

Flame of El, light of God. The archangel of light and wisdom. In 1 Enoch, Uri'el is the angel who guides Chanoch through the heavenly realms and reveals the secrets of the sun, moon, stars, and the 364-day solar calendar. His role as keeper of the celestial lights makes him foundational to the Qumran calendar system. The Astronomical Book of Enoch (1 Enoch 72-82) is explicitly structured as Uri'el's teaching to Chanoch. Uri'el is the archangel most directly connected to the DSS solar calendar and cosmological framework.

The goat that departs, or fierce one of God. Two meanings in scripture: (1) In Vayikra 16 the scapegoat sent into the wilderness carrying Yisrael's sins. (2) In 1 Enoch 8-10, Azazel is the leader of the fallen Watchers who taught humanity metalworking, weapons, and cosmetics, corrupting the earth. YHWH commands Refa'el to bind Azazel hand and foot and bury him in the desert of Dudael until the final judgment. The DSS Book of Giants (4Q203) from Qumran names Azazel prominently. He is the primary antagonist of the DSS cosmological drama.

My name has seen, or name of the vision. The leader of the 200 Watchers (B'nei Elohim) who descended on Mount Hermon and took human wives in 1 Enoch 6. Shemihazah led the oath — all 200 Watchers bound themselves by mutual oath before descending, so none could withdraw. Their union produced the Nephilim (giants). YHWH bound Shemihazah and the Watchers under the earth for 70 generations until the final judgment. The Book of Giants (4Q531) from Qumran deals extensively with Shemihazah and the consequences of the Watcher descent.

The title the late Qumran sect gave its own founder-figure, referred to by title rather than name. He is no covenant figure — he appears nowhere in the covenant record and is named only in the sect's own sectarian rulebooks, the Damascus Document and the Habakkuk Pesher, which cast him as a priest who "received direct revelation" and was persecuted by their "Wicked Priest." The covenant record's own teacher of righteousness is not a breakaway human founder but YHWH Himself — "I am YHWH your Creator, who teaches you to profit" (Yeshayahu 48:17), and "your Teacher will not hide himself, and your eyes shall see your Teacher" (Yeshayahu 30:20) — with His true priest, in whose mouth is true instruction and whose lips guard knowledge, for he is the messenger of YHWH (Malakhi 2:6-7), and the prophet like Moshe raised up from among the people (Devarim 18:15). The Qumran figure is the self-mythologizing legend of one breakaway faction, later seized on by Christian claim-making to prop up the NT's invented figure. Not found in the authentic record. A later addition of manipulation texts.

A title the late Qumran sect invented for its own enemy — the Jerusalem high priest it cast as the persecutor of its founder-figure, the so-called "Teacher of Righteousness." It appears nowhere in the covenant record; it is named only in the sect's own Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab 8-12), which paints him as one who began in truth, turned arrogant, betrayed Torah, and hunted the Teacher on Yom Kippur. One breakaway faction's factional legend — a 1st-century-BCE sectarian construct, not covenant history. Not found in the authentic record. A later addition of manipulation texts.

key_terms.term: Man of the Lie / Ish HaKazav
key_terms.definition: A title in the late sect's own rulebooks — the Damascus Document and the pesharim — for an internal rival the faction accused of leading people from its reading of Torah and rejecting its founder-figure, the "Teacher of Righteousness" (CD 20:15, "he dripped lies to Yisrael"). It is the sect's own factional polemic against a breakaway leader, named nowhere in the covenant record. A 1st-century-BCE sectarian construct, not covenant scripture. Not found in the authentic record. A later addition of manipulation texts.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for YHWH?
faq.answer: English: YHWH | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: יהוה | Transliteration: YHWH | Root letters: י-ה-ו-ה | Category: names | meaning: The name of the Creator. Four consonants, the Tetragrammaton. Appears 6,828 times in the Hebrew Bible. Present in the 1QIsa-a Great Isaiah Scroll and throughout the Dead Sea Scrolls. Not a title — the personal name.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Israel / Yisrael?
faq.answer: English: Israel / Yisrael | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤔𐤓𐤀𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: יִשְׂרָאֵל | Transliteration: Yisra'el | Root letters: ש-ר-ה + א-ל | Category: names | meaning: Wrestled with El. Name given to Yaakov in Bereshit 32:29. Refers to the people of the covenant. Attested across DSS texts including 1QIsa-a and 4QDeut.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Jerusalem / Yerushalayim?
faq.answer: English: Jerusalem / Yerushalayim | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤓𐤅𐤔𐤋𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: יְרוּשָׁלַיִם | Transliteration: Yerushalayim | Root letters: י-ר-ש + ש-ל-מ | Category: names | meaning: City of peace, or foundation of peace. Capital city of the covenant people — the stronghold of Tziyon that Dawid took and called the city of Dawid (Shmuel Bet 5:7), the city YHWH chose to put His name and desired for His dwelling place (Melakhim Bet 21:4; Tehillim 132:13). YHWH loves the gates of Tziyon (Tehillim 87:2); it is the joy of all the earth, the city of the great King (Tehillim 48:2), and out of it goes the Torah (Yeshayahu 2:3). Pray for the peace of Yerushalayim (Tehillim 122:6); if I forget you, O Yerushalayim, let my right hand forget its skill (Tehillim 137:5).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Egypt / Mitzrayim?
faq.answer: English: Egypt / Mitzrayim | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤑𐤓𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: מִצְרַיִם | Transliteration: Mitzrayim | Root letters: צ-ר-ר | Category: names | meaning: Dual form suggesting two regions (Upper and Lower). Place of bondage referenced in Devarim 28:68 and the Exodus narrative throughout the DSS.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Enoch / Chanokh?
faq.answer: English: Enoch / Chanokh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤍𐤅𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: חֲנוֹךְ | Transliteration: Chanokh | Root letters: ח-נ-כ | Category: names | meaning: Dedicated, initiated. Seventh from Adam. Taken by YHWH without dying (Bereshit 5:24). Author of 1 Enoch, one of the most-copied texts at Qumran. DSS fragments: 4Q201-212.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for covenant / brit?
faq.answer: English: covenant / brit | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤓𐤉𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: בְּרִית | Transliteration: berit | Root letters: ב-ר-ת | Category: covenant | meaning: Covenant, binding agreement. Central term of the entire DSS corpus. Used in Bereshit 15 (covenant with Avraham), Devarim 28-30 (blessings and curses), and throughout the Damascus Document and Community Rule.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Torah / instruction?
faq.answer: English: Torah / instruction | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤕𐤅𐤓𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: תּוֹרָה | Transliteration: Torah | Root letters: י-ר-ה | Category: covenant | meaning: Teaching, instruction. From the root meaning to shoot or direct. The five books of Moshe. Called Orit in Ge'ez. DSS texts treat Torah as the binding covenant document — not as rabbinic law.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for commandment / mitzvah?
faq.answer: English: commandment / mitzvah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤑𐤅𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: מִצְוָה | Transliteration: mitzvah | Root letters: צ-ו-ה | Category: covenant | meaning: Commandment, directive. From the root to command. The specific instructions of YHWH. The DSS and Orit treat each commandment as an element of the covenant relationship, not a religious ritual.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Sabbath / Shabbat?
faq.answer: English: Sabbath / Shabbat | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤁𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: שַׁבָּת | Transliteration: Shabbat | Root letters: ש-ב-ת | Category: covenant | meaning: Rest, cessation. From the root to stop. The seventh day, sanctified at creation (Bereshit 2:2-3). The DSS 364-day solar calendar keeps Shabbat on a fixed day every week without drift. The covenant record sets the specific Shabbat laws directly (Shemot 20:8-11; 35:3; 16:29; Amos 8:5; Yirmeyahu 17:21-22).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for righteousness / tzedek?
faq.answer: English: righteousness / tzedek | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤑𐤃𐤒 | Modern Hebrew: צֶדֶק | Transliteration: tzedek | Root letters: צ-ד-ק | Category: covenant | meaning: Righteousness, justice, rightness. One of the core covenant virtues, and YHWH's own character: "For YHWH is righteous — he loves righteous deeds — the upright shall behold his face" (Tehillim 11:7); "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne" (Tehillim 89:14). The coming Davidic king carries it as his very name: "this is the name by which he will be called: YHWH Is Our Righteousness" (Yirmeyahu 23:6). Found throughout Tehillim and the Prophets in DSS form.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for justice / mishpat?
faq.answer: English: justice / mishpat | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤔𐤐𐤈 | Modern Hebrew: מִשְׁפָּט | Transliteration: mishpat | Root letters: ש-פ-ט | Category: covenant | meaning: Judgment, justice, ordinance, legal ruling. Paired with tzedek throughout the Prophets. The covenant record sets mishpat as YHWH's own judgment: He judges the world in righteousness and the peoples with uprightness (Tehillim 9:8; 96:13; 98:9); He gathers the nations to the Valley of Yehoshafat to enter into judgment with them (Yoel 3:2,12); He draws near for judgment as a swift witness against the wicked (Malakhi 3:5); and He brings every deed into judgment, with every secret thing (Kohelet 12:14). Also means legal case or custom.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for lovingkindness / chesed?
faq.answer: English: lovingkindness / chesed | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤎𐤃 | Modern Hebrew: חֶסֶד | Transliteration: chesed | Root letters: ח-ס-ד | Category: covenant | meaning: Covenant loyalty, lovingkindness, steadfast love. Often translated mercy. Describes YHWH's faithfulness to the covenant. Not mere emotion but relational obligation. Central in Tehillim and Hoshea.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for truth / emet?
faq.answer: English: truth / emet | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤌𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: אֱמֶת | Transliteration: emet | Root letters: א-מ-נ | Category: covenant | meaning: Truth, faithfulness, reliability. Related to amen. Describes both factual truth and covenantal trustworthiness. Often paired with chesed in Tehillim and the Prophets.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for blessing / berakhah?
faq.answer: English: blessing / berakhah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤓𐤊𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: בְּרָכָה | Transliteration: berakhah | Root letters: ב-ר-כ | Category: covenant | meaning: Blessing, gift of increase. The covenant blessings of Devarim 28:1-14 are conditional on obedience. The root barak also means to kneel, suggesting reverence in receiving.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for curse / kelalah?
faq.answer: English: curse / kelalah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤒𐤋𐤋𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: קְלָלָה | Transliteration: kelalah | Root letters: ק-ל-ל | Category: covenant | meaning: Curse, diminishment. The covenant curses of Devarim 28:15-68 follow disobedience. The DSS 4QDeut fragments attest the curse passage. Verse 68 describes return to Egypt by ships — interpreted in DSS context as the transatlantic slave trade by some scholars.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for redemption / geulah (covenant #1)?
faq.answer: English: redemption / geulah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤂𐤀𐤅𐤋𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: גְּאֻלָּה | Transliteration: geulah | Root letters: ג-א-ל | Category: covenant | meaning: Redemption, buying back. The go'el is the kinsman-redeemer who restores what was lost. Used of YHWH redeeming Yisrael from Egypt and referenced in 11Q13 Melchizedek scroll for the final jubilee redemption.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for repentance / teshuvah?
faq.answer: English: repentance / teshuvah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤕𐤔𐤅𐤁𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: תְּשׁוּבָה | Transliteration: teshuvah | Root letters: ש-ו-ב | Category: covenant | meaning: Return, turning back. From the verb shuv, to return. Repentance in DSS/Orit is a physical return to covenant obedience — returning to YHWH's commandments — not only an inner spiritual state.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for holiness / kodesh?
faq.answer: English: holiness / kodesh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤒𐤃𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: קֹדֶשׁ | Transliteration: kodesh | Root letters: ק-ד-ש | Category: worship | meaning: Holiness, separateness, set-apartness. What belongs to YHWH. Vayikra 19:2: You shall be holy, for I YHWH your Creator am holy. Yeshayahu 6:3 shows the holy ones in the heavenly sanctuary proclaiming Holy, holy, holy is YHWH of hosts. Used in the Shema-connected texts.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for praise / hallel?
faq.answer: English: praise / hallel | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤋𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: הַלֵּל | Transliteration: hallel | Root letters: ה-ל-ל | Category: worship | meaning: Praise, shine, be radiant. The basis of HalleluYah (Praise YHWH). The Psalms/Tehillim use this root throughout. 11QPs (Cave 11 Psalms Scroll) contains halleluyah psalms in a different order from the Masoretic text.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for HalleluYah?
faq.answer: English: HalleluYah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤋𐤋𐤅𐤉𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: הַלְלוּיָהּ | Transliteration: HalleluYah | Root letters: ה-ל-ל + י-ה | Category: worship | meaning: Praise YHWH. A direct command form of hallel joined with Yah, the short form of YHWH's name. Appears throughout Tehillim (Psalms) in DSS form. Not a generic exclamation — an instruction to praise the Creator by name.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for prayer / tefillah?
