faq.answer: English: prayer / tefillah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤕𐤐𐤋𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: תְּפִלָּה | Transliteration: tefillah | Root letters: פ-ל-ל | Category: worship | meaning: Prayer, supplication, intercession. The covenant record carries it directly — five Tehillim are titled tefillah, including Tehillim 90 "A tefillah of Moshe" and Tehillim 86 "A tefillah of David." The root palal means to judge or intervene, suggesting prayer as seeking YHWH's intervention.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for sacrifice / korban?
faq.answer: English: sacrifice / korban | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤒𐤓𐤁𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: קָרְבָּן | Transliteration: korban | Root letters: ק-ר-ב | Category: worship | meaning: Offering, that which is brought near. From karav, to draw near. The covenant record details the proper offerings (Vayikra 1-7; Bamidbar 28-29). The root expresses approach to YHWH through the act of bringing an offering.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for atonement / kippur?
faq.answer: English: atonement / kippur | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤊𐤐𐤅𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: כִּפּוּר | Transliteration: kippur | Root letters: כ-פ-ר | Category: worship | meaning: Covering, atonement, ransom. Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement. The root kfr means to cover or wipe clean. Vayikra 16 sets the Day of Atonement rite in the covenant record.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Shema / hear?
faq.answer: English: Shema / hear | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌𐤏 | Modern Hebrew: שְׁמַע | Transliteration: Shema | Root letters: ש-מ-ע | Category: worship | meaning: Hear, listen, obey. The command that opens Devarim 6:4: Shema Yisrael YHWH Eloheinu YHWH Echad. The Nash Papyrus (2nd century BCE) is the oldest known manuscript of this text. In Hebrew, hearing implies obeying.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for spirit / ruach?
faq.answer: English: spirit / ruach | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤓𐤅𐤇 | Modern Hebrew: רוּחַ | Transliteration: ruach | Root letters: ר-ו-ח | Category: creation | meaning: Wind, breath, spirit. In Bereshit 1:2 the ruach of YHWH moves over the face of the waters. In DSS texts the ruach is the animating force of life and the vehicle of prophetic revelation. Not a separate divine person in the DSS framework.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for light / or?
faq.answer: English: light / or | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤅𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: אוֹר | Transliteration: or | Root letters: א-ו-ר | Category: creation | meaning: Light. First creation in Bereshit 1:3. Tehillim 119:105 names the word of YHWH a lamp to the feet and an or (light) to the path. Also the name of revelation — Torah is or for the path.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for darkness / choshekh?
faq.answer: English: darkness / choshekh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤔𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: חֹשֶׁךְ | Transliteration: choshekh | Root letters: ח-ש-כ | Category: creation | meaning: Darkness. Present before creation (Bereshit 1:2). In the late sectarian 1QS/1QM (later manipulated additions) a personified “Belial” was said to rule the sons of darkness. In the primary Orit, darkness is the pre-creation state and moral corruption, not a demon-king. Also used of moral corruption.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for heaven / shamayim?
faq.answer: English: heaven / shamayim | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: שָׁמַיִם | Transliteration: shamayim | Root letters: ש-מ-י | Category: creation | meaning: Heavens, sky. Dual form in Hebrew. Created on day two in Bereshit 1:6-8. 1 Enoch chapters 17-36 describe Enoch's tour of the heavens. Not described in DSS texts as a post-death dwelling for humans — YHWH's domain.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for earth / eretz?
faq.answer: English: earth / eretz | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤓𐤑 | Modern Hebrew: אֶרֶץ | Transliteration: eretz | Root letters: א-ר-צ | Category: creation | meaning: Earth, land, ground. Created in Bereshit 1:1. Also specifically the Land promised in the covenant. The DSS texts use eretz for both the planet and the specific covenant land.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for water / mayim?
faq.answer: English: water / mayim | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: מַיִם | Transliteration: mayim | Root letters: מ-י-מ | Category: creation | meaning: Water. Dual or plural form, always plural in Hebrew. Present at creation (Bereshit 1:2). The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) and 1 Enoch both describe the primordial waters. Also used for Torah as living water.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for fire / esh?
faq.answer: English: fire / esh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: אֵשׁ | Transliteration: esh | Root letters: א-ש | Category: creation | meaning: Fire. YHWH appears in fire at Sinai (Shemot 19:18) and to Moshe in the burning bush. 1 Enoch 14:8-23 describes the heavenly throne as fire. The pit of fire in 1 Enoch 10:13 is the prison of the Watchers.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for soul / nefesh (creation #1)?
faq.answer: English: soul / nefesh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤍𐤐𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ | Transliteration: nefesh | Root letters: נ-פ-ש | Category: creation | meaning: Soul, living being, self. In Bereshit 2:7 YHWH breathes into Adam and he becomes a living nefesh. In 1 Enoch 22 the nefesh of the dead wait at rest in four chambers in Sheol — not in heaven. Death is real: the dead rest in Sheol awaiting the judgment, not an immediate ascent — yet they are not extinguished, for Shmuel was roused from that rest and spoke to Sha'ul (1 Shemuel 28:15).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for name / shem?
faq.answer: English: name / shem | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: שֵׁם | Transliteration: shem | Root letters: ש-מ | Category: names | meaning: Name, reputation, memorial. Also the name of Noah's son Shem (ancestor of Semitic peoples). YHWH's name is holy and set apart. The suppression of YHWH's name in Greek translations (replaced by Kyrios/Lord) is documented from 200 BCE onward.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for word / davar?
faq.answer: English: word / davar | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤁𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: דָּבָר | Transliteration: davar | Root letters: ד-ב-ר | Category: covenant | meaning: Word, thing, matter. YHWH's davar goes forth and accomplishes its purpose (Yeshayahu 55:11). The Ten Commandments are the ten Devarim (words/things). Torah as the spoken-then-written word of YHWH.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for wisdom / chokhmah?
faq.answer: English: wisdom / chokhmah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤊𐤌𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: חָכְמָה | Transliteration: chokhmah | Root letters: ח-כ-מ | Category: dssterms | meaning: Wisdom. Central virtue of Mishlei (Proverbs) and DSS wisdom texts. 4QInstruction is the largest DSS wisdom text, teaching practical daily life grounded in the raz nihyeh (mystery of existence). Wisdom is relational knowledge of YHWH's ways, not mere intelligence.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for knowledge / daat?
faq.answer: English: knowledge / daat | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤏𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: דַּעַת | Transliteration: daat | Root letters: ד-ע-ת | Category: dssterms | meaning: Knowledge, intimate knowing. From the verb yada, to know deeply. In Bereshit 2:17 the tree of knowledge of good and evil. The DSS 4QInstruction uses raz nihyeh (mystery of existence) as the ultimate object of daat.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for mystery / raz?
faq.answer: English: mystery / raz | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤓𐤆 | Modern Hebrew: רָז | Transliteration: raz | Root letters: ר-ז | Category: dssterms | meaning: Mystery, secret. An Aramaic loanword appearing throughout DSS texts. 4QInstruction uses raz nihyeh (the mystery of what is to come/the mystery of existence) as its central concept — the hidden structure of reality that the wise one studies to understand daily life.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for community / yachad?
faq.answer: English: community / yachad | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤇𐤃 | Modern Hebrew: יַחַד | Transliteration: yachad | Root letters: י-ח-ד | Category: dssterms | meaning: Together, community, unity. The name the Qumran covenant community used for itself, drawn straight from the covenant record — Devarim 33:5 sets the tribes of Israel yachad (together) under YHWH as King, and Tehillim 133:1 blesses brothers who dwell together (gam yachad). Emphasizes communal covenant renewal, separation from outsiders, and collective obedience.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for lot / destiny / goral?
faq.answer: English: lot / destiny / goral | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤂𐤅𐤓𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: גּוֹרָל | Transliteration: goral | Root letters: ג-ו-ר | Category: dssterms | meaning: Lot, destiny, portion. In the covenant record the lot is cast, but its every decision is from YHWH (Mishlei 16:33): the land was divided among the tribes by lot (Bamidbar 26:55), and the two goats of Yom Kippur were set by lot, one for YHWH and one for Azazel (Vayikra 16:8). Each person's lot is set before them — life and light, or death and darkness (Devarim 30:19): the path of the righteous is the light of dawn, shining brighter and brighter (Mishlei 4:18; Tehillim 97:11), while the way of the wicked is deep darkness (Mishlei 4:19). YHWH Himself holds a person's portion and lot (Tehillim 16:5).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Watcher / ir?
faq.answer: English: Watcher / ir | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤏𐤉𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: עִיר | Transliteration: ir | Root letters: ע-ו-ר | Category: dssterms | meaning: Watcher, holy one. The angelic beings who descended to earth in 1 Enoch 6-11 and the Book of Giants (4Q203). 200 Watchers led by Shemihaza descended on Mount Hermon. The name means one who watches or stays awake. Their fall introduces evil into the world.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Belial / worthlessness?
faq.answer: English: Belial / worthlessness | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤋𐤉𐤏𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: בְּלִיַּעַל | Transliteration: Belial | Root letters: ב-ל-ע + י-ע-ל | Category: dssterms | meaning: Worthlessness, without profit (beli + ya'al). In the pre-exilic Hebrew Orit it is an abstract adjective for human lawbreakers and traitors (Devarim 13:13, Shoftim 19:22, 1 Shemuel 1:16). Its personification into a cosmic prince of darkness is a late Second Temple sectarian development (1QS, CD, 1QM) — later manipulated additions, not covenant text. Distinct from HaSatan. The Damascus Document warns against the three nets of Belial: fornication, wealth, and defilement of the sanctuary.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for angel / messenger / malach?
faq.answer: English: angel / messenger / malach | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤋𐤀𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ | Transliteration: malach | Root letters: מ-ל-א-כ | Category: creation | meaning: Messenger, angel. From the root meaning work/task. A malach is a sent being with an assigned office, never an independent deity. The covenant record names them and their functions. Mikha'el is the chief prince and war-guardian of the covenant people: Daniyel 10:13, "Mikha'el, one of the chief princes, came to help me"; 12:1, "Mikha'el, the great prince who has charge of your people... your people shall be delivered." Gavri'el is the interpreter of visions: Daniyel 8:16, "Gavri'el, make this man understand the vision." The commander of the army of YHWH stands over His host (Yehoshua 5:14). One angel is sent to guard the way (Shemot 23:20) and to guard the covenant people in all their ways (Tehillim 91:11). Others execute judgment: the destroyer at Passover (Shemot 12:23) and the angel who struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of Assyria in a single night (Melakhim Bet 19:35). The cherubim guard the holy with a flaming sword (Bereshit 3:24); the serafim attend the throne and cry Holy, holy, holy (Yeshayahu 6:2-3). The faithful host do his word, obeying the voice of his word (Tehillim 103:20), are made winds and flaming fire (Tehillim 104:4), and praise Him as beings He created at His command (Tehillim 148:2,5). The Watchers transgressed their appointed boundary and did what they wanted, and were bound for judgment (Book of the Watchers, 1 Chanokh). Obedient or fallen, every malach is a created being with a specific task, never an independent deity.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Jubilee / yovel?
faq.answer: English: Jubilee / yovel | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤅𐤁𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: יוֹבֵל | Transliteration: yovel | Root letters: י-ב-ל | Category: covenant | meaning: Jubilee, ram's horn, year of release. Every 50th year in Vayikra 25. 11QMelchizedek uses jubilee timing for the final redemption.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Passover / Pesach?
faq.answer: English: Passover / Pesach | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤐𐤎𐤇 | Modern Hebrew: פֶּסַח | Transliteration: Pesach | Root letters: פ-ס-ח | Category: worship | meaning: Passover, to pass over. The night YHWH passed over the houses marked with blood in Egypt (Shemot 12). The Qumran calendar places Pesach on different dates from the Pharisaic calendar due to the 364-day solar year. The DSS community observed it as a covenant renewal.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for temple / heikhal?
faq.answer: English: temple / heikhal | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤉𐤊𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: הֵיכָל | Transliteration: heikhal | Root letters: ה-י-כ-ל | Category: worship | meaning: Temple, palace, hall. The inner hall of the sanctuary. The covenant record gives YHWH's own instructions for the sanctuary — the Mishkan pattern shown to Moshe (Shemot 25-31), the temple Shlomo built (Melakhim Aleph 6-7), and the visionary temple of Yechezkel 40-48. The Qumran community treated their own assembly as a living substitute for the defiled Jerusalem temple.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for ark / aron?
faq.answer: English: ark / aron | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤓𐤅𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: אָרוֹן | Transliteration: aron | Root letters: א-ר-נ | Category: worship | meaning: Ark, chest, box. The Ark of the Covenant (Aron HaBrit) housed the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. The covenant record places it last in the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place of Shlomo's temple (Melakhim Aleph 8:6); Yirmeyahu declared it would no longer be spoken of, remembered, or made again (Yirmeyahu 3:16). It has not been seen since the Babylonian destruction.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for sign / ot?
faq.answer: English: sign / ot | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤅𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: אוֹת | Transliteration: ot | Root letters: א-ו-ת | Category: covenant | meaning: Sign, mark, token. The rainbow is the ot of the Noachide covenant (Bereshit 9:12). Tzitzit (fringes) are an ot of the covenant (Bamidbar 15:39). The Shabbat is an ot between YHWH and Yisrael forever (Shemot 31:13). Also: the first letter, Aleph, is itself named ot.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for remembrance / zikaron?
faq.answer: English: remembrance / zikaron | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤆𐤊𐤓𐤅𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: זִכָּרוֹן | Transliteration: zikaron | Root letters: ז-כ-ר | Category: covenant | meaning: Remembrance, memorial. YHWH commands Israel to remember the Exodus, the Sabbath, and the covenant. The root zakhar means to remember and to act on what is remembered. In DSS texts, forgetting the covenant is the root of the curse of Devarim 28.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for exile / galut?
faq.answer: English: exile / galut | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤂𐤋𐤅𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: גָּלוּת | Transliteration: galut | Root letters: ג-ל-ה | Category: covenant | meaning: Exile, captivity, dispersal. The covenant curses of Devarim 28 culminate in exile. The DSS community understood themselves as living in a form of exile. The Damascus Document (CD) opens describing the exile of the covenant people and their flight to Damascus.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for return / shuv?
faq.answer: English: return / shuv | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤅𐤁 | Modern Hebrew: שׁוּב | Transliteration: shuv | Root letters: ש-ו-ב | Category: covenant | meaning: To return, turn back. The action word of repentance. In Devarim 30:2 YHWH promises restoration when the people shuv (return) to him with all their heart. DSS texts treat shuv as the central act of covenant renewal.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for heart / lev?
faq.answer: English: heart / lev | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤋𐤁 | Modern Hebrew: לֵב | Transliteration: lev | Root letters: ל-ב | Category: daily | meaning: Heart, mind, inner person. In ancient Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of reason and will, not just emotion. Shema Yisrael requires love with all your heart (Devarim 6:5). Tehillim 24:3-4 sets who may ascend the mountain of YHWH — the one with clean hands and a pure heart (bar levav); Devarim 10:16 commands to circumcise the foreskin of the heart.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for soul / nefesh (daily #2)?
faq.answer: English: soul / nefesh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤍𐤐𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ | Transliteration: nefesh | Root letters: נ-פ-ש | Category: daily | meaning: Living being, person, appetite, life. Devarim 6:5 commands love with all your nefesh. In 1 Enoch 22 the nefesh of the righteous and wicked wait in separate chambers in Sheol. Not an immortal essence — the nefesh that sins dies (Yehezkel 18:20).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for hand / yad?
faq.answer: English: hand / yad | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤃 | Modern Hebrew: יָד | Transliteration: yad | Root letters: י-ד | Category: daily | meaning: Hand, power, authority. Shemot 13:9 says the commandments are a sign on your hand. Tzitzit cords are tied on the hands. Also used metaphorically for YHWH's power — the hand of YHWH. The letter Yod (the smallest Hebrew letter) is the first letter of YHWH.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for eye / ayin?
faq.answer: English: eye / ayin | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤏𐤉𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: עַיִן | Transliteration: ayin | Root letters: ע-י-נ | Category: daily | meaning: Eye, spring of water, appearance. Devarim 6:8 says the commandments are frontlets between your eyes. Also the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (𐤏). A spring or source of water shares this name — what the eye and a spring have in common is they both reveal what is beneath.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for bread / lechem?
faq.answer: English: bread / lechem | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤋𐤇𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: לֶחֶם | Transliteration: lechem | Root letters: ל-ח-מ | Category: daily | meaning: Bread, food, sustenance. Shemot 16 — the manna in the wilderness. Shemot 24:11 records the covenant meal — after the covenant was sealed, the elders ate and drank before YHWH; Bereshit 14:18 shows Malki-Tzedek, priest of the Most High, bringing out bread and wine. The bread of presence (lechem ha-panim) was set before YHWH in the sanctuary continuously.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for blood / dam?
faq.answer: English: blood / dam | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: דָּם | Transliteration: dam | Root letters: ד-מ | Category: daily | meaning: Blood. Life is in the blood (Vayikra 17:11). Covenant ratification involved blood (Shemot 24:8). The prohibition on consuming blood is found throughout Vayikra and in the Damascus Document (CD 12:13). The Devarim 28:68 slave trade involved the shedding of blood.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for life / chayyim?
faq.answer: English: life / chayyim | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤉𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: חַיִּים | Transliteration: chayyim | Root letters: ח-י-ה | Category: daily | meaning: Life, living. Always plural in Hebrew. YHWH is El Chayyim, the living Creator. The Torah is eitz chayyim (tree of life) to those who hold it. Devarim 30:19-20 sets YHWH as the source of the covenant people's life — "choose life... for He is your life and the length of your days."

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for death / mavet?
faq.answer: English: death / mavet | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤅𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: מָוֶת | Transliteration: mavet | Root letters: מ-ו-ת | Category: daily | meaning: Death. The nefesh that sins dies (Yehezkel 18:20). Death is real: the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to the Creator who gave it (Kohelet 12:7). It is no immediate passage to heaven — the dead are in Sheol below, from which Shmuel was brought up and spoke to Sha'ul, knowing him and foretelling that tomorrow he and his sons would be with him (1 Shemuel 28:15,19). YHWH will swallow up death forever and wipe away every tear (Yeshayahu 25:8). Moshe died and was buried by YHWH (Devarim 34:6).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for peace / shalom?
faq.answer: English: peace / shalom | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤋𐤅𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: שָׁלוֹם | Transliteration: shalom | Root letters: ש-ל-מ | Category: daily | meaning: Peace, wholeness, completeness. Not just absence of conflict but total flourishing. The covenant blessings include shalom. Used as a greeting in the DSS texts. The root shalem means to be complete or to make payment — shalom is the state of everything being in right order.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for sin / chet?
faq.answer: English: sin / chet | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤈𐤀 | Modern Hebrew: חֵטְא | Transliteration: chet | Root letters: ח-ט-א | Category: covenant | meaning: Sin, missing the mark. From the root meaning to miss a target. Shemot 34:7 and Vayikra 16:21 name the three categories together — chet (sin), pesha (rebellion), and avon (iniquity). Distinct from pesha (rebellion/transgression) and avon (iniquity/twisted action). Covenant violation in DSS is measured against specific commandments.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for servant / eved?
faq.answer: English: servant / eved | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤏𐤁𐤃 | Modern Hebrew: עֶבֶד | Transliteration: eved | Root letters: ע-ב-ד | Category: covenant | meaning: Servant, slave, worker. Also worshiper — to serve and to worship share the same root (avad). The covenant people are described as servants of YHWH. In Devarim 28:68 the curse warns of being sold as servants — the slave trade passage. Avad also means to work the land.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for shepherd / ro'eh?
faq.answer: English: shepherd / ro'eh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤓𐤅𐤏𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: רֹעֶה | Transliteration: ro'eh | Root letters: ר-ע-ה | Category: daily | meaning: Shepherd, herdsman. YHWH is described as shepherd in Tehillim 23. Moshe, David, and the patriarchs were shepherds. The DSS Damascus Document uses shepherd imagery for community leaders. The root r'h also means to see and to pasture — a shepherd sees and feeds.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for prophet / navi?
faq.answer: English: prophet / navi | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤍𐤁𐤉𐤀 | Modern Hebrew: נָבִיא | Transliteration: navi | Root letters: נ-ב-א | Category: covenant | meaning: Prophet, spokesperson. One called to speak YHWH's words to the people. Devarim 13:1-5 gives the test: a prophet who teaches violation of Torah is false regardless of signs. The DSS Pesher texts interpret classical prophecy as being fulfilled in their own era.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for priest / kohen?
faq.answer: English: priest / kohen | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤊𐤄𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: כֹּהֵן | Transliteration: kohen | Root letters: כ-ה-נ | Category: worship | meaning: Priest. From the tribe of Levi, specifically Aaronite descent. The Qumran community was led by priests — the Sons of Zadok (kohanim). The covenant record details the priestly duties — the consecration of Aharon and his sons, their garments, and their charge (Shemot 28-29; Vayikra 8-10; Bamidbar 18).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for king / melech?
faq.answer: English: king / melech | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤋𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: מֶלֶךְ | Transliteration: melech | Root letters: מ-ל-כ | Category: names | meaning: King, ruler. YHWH alone is King: "I am YHWH, your Holy One, the Creator of Yisra'EL, your King" (Yeshayahu 43:15); "YHWH is our judge, YHWH is our lawgiver, YHWH is our king — he will save us" (Yeshayahu 33:22); "YHWH is King forever and ever" (Tehillim 10:16); "YHWH reigns — he is robed in majesty" (Tehillim 93:1). The kingdom is His: "For kingship belongs to YHWH, and he rules over the nations" (Tehillim 22:28); "Yours is the kingdom, O YHWH, and you are exalted as head above all" (Divrei HaYamim Aleph 29:11). In 1 Samuel 8 the people's demand for a human king was a rejection of YHWH's kingship — "when YHWH your Creator was your king" (1 Shemuel 12:12). The covenant record foretells the coming Davidic king under YHWH: "There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Yishai" (Yeshayahu 11:1); "I will raise up for Dawid a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king" (Yirmeyahu 23:5); "My servant Dawid shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd" (Yechezkel 34:23-24). And YHWH shuts the door on every rival king, savior, or deity — including the Roman-era invented Yeshua figure set up as king and god: "the King of Yisra'EL and his Redeemer, YHWH of hosts: I am the first and I am the last — besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 44:6); "I, I am YHWH, and besides me there is no savior" (Yeshayahu 43:11); "I am YHWH, and there is no other. Besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 45:5); "Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth. For I am Creator, and there is no other" (Yeshayahu 45:22); "you know no Creator but me, and besides me there is no savior" (Hoshea 13:4); "YHWH is The Creator — there is no other besides him" (Devarim 4:35). No man is that deity: "The Creator is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind" (Bamidbar 23:19). To crown any other is idolatry: "You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I YHWH your Creator am a jealous Creator" (Shemot 20:5); "I am YHWH — that is my name. My glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols" (Yeshayahu 42:8); "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands" (Tehillim 115:4).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for father / av?
faq.answer: English: father / av | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤁 | Modern Hebrew: אָב | Transliteration: av | Root letters: א-ב | Category: daily | meaning: Father. Also the letter Aleph-Bet (Aleph + Bet = father). YHWH is described as father of Yisrael (Devarim 32:6). The patriarchs (avot) are Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. The word av is one of the first words a child learns in Hebrew.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for mother / em?
faq.answer: English: mother / em | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: אֵם | Transliteration: em | Root letters: א-מ | Category: daily | meaning: Mother. The root em also means people/nation. Honoring father and mother (av ve'em) is the fifth commandment (Shemot 20:12). Also related to emet (truth) — the mother as the foundation of the household. The word am (people) may derive from the same root.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for son / ben?
faq.answer: English: son / ben | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: בֵּן | Transliteration: ben | Root letters: ב-נ | Category: daily | meaning: Son, child, member of a group. Bereshit opens with YHWH creating the heavens and earth and the human family begins. Ben can also mean a member of a category — b'nei Yisrael (sons of Israel = the Israelite people), b'nei Elohim (sons of God = angels in 1 Enoch 6).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for daughter / bat?
faq.answer: English: daughter / bat | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: בַּת | Transliteration: bat | Root letters: ב-ת | Category: daily | meaning: Daughter. Feminine form of ben. Bat Yisrael (daughter of Israel) — a term for the covenant women. The daughters of the Yachad community at Qumran are mentioned in the Damascus Document. Also used metaphorically — Bat Tzion (daughter of Zion) for Jerusalem.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for house / bayit?
faq.answer: English: house / bayit | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤉𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: בַּיִת | Transliteration: bayit | Root letters: ב-י-ת | Category: daily | meaning: House, household, temple. Beit YHWH is the house of YHWH — the sanctuary. Beit Yisrael is the house of Israel. The covenant is made with households, not just individuals. The letter Bet (𐤁) means house — it is the second letter and the first letter of Bereshit (In the beginning).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for day / yom?
faq.answer: English: day / yom | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤅𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: יוֹם | Transliteration: yom | Root letters: י-ו-מ | Category: daily | meaning: Day. In the DSS 364-day solar calendar, days begin at sunrise (not sunset as in rabbinic tradition). Yom Kippur, Yom HaBikkurim and other holy days fall on fixed days of the week in the DSS calendar, never drifting to different weekdays as in the lunar calendar.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for night / laylah?
faq.answer: English: night / laylah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤋𐤉𐤋𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: לַיְלָה | Transliteration: laylah | Root letters: ל-י-ל | Category: daily | meaning: Night. In Bereshit 1 evening and morning mark each creation day. The Shabbat in DSS runs sunrise to sunrise, making night part of the new day — distinct from the rabbinic sunset-to-sunset tradition. 1 Enoch describes the angel of night keeping watch.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for year / shanah?
faq.answer: English: year / shanah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤍𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: שָׁנָה | Transliteration: shanah | Root letters: ש-נ-ה | Category: daily | meaning: Year, repetition. The DSS 364-day solar year has exactly 52 weeks, keeping every festival on the same day of the week every year. The root shanah also means to repeat or to change.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for month / chodesh?
faq.answer: English: month / chodesh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤃𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: חֹדֶשׁ | Transliteration: chodesh | Root letters: ח-ד-ש | Category: daily | meaning: Month, new thing. Related to chadash (new). In the DSS 364-day calendar, each month has 30 days and seasons are separated by an intercalary day (91 days per quarter). This differs from the lunar calendar which adds days to match the moon cycle.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for mountain / har?
faq.answer: English: mountain / har | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: הַר | Transliteration: har | Root letters: ה-ר | Category: creation | meaning: Mountain. Har Sinai (Mount Sinai) where Torah was given. Har Hermon where the Watchers descended in 1 Enoch 6:6. Har HaBayit (Temple Mount) in Jerusalem. Mountains in DSS texts are both geographical and cosmic — boundary points between earth and heaven.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for wilderness / midbar?
faq.answer: English: wilderness / midbar | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤃𐤁𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: מִדְבָּר | Transliteration: midbar | Root letters: ד-ב-ר | Category: creation | meaning: Wilderness, desert, place of speaking. The root is davar (word). The wilderness is where YHWH speaks. The Yachad community went to the wilderness of Judea specifically (citing Yeshayahu 40:3: prepare the way of YHWH in the wilderness).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for sea / yam?
faq.answer: English: sea / yam | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: יָם | Transliteration: yam | Root letters: י-מ | Category: creation | meaning: Sea, west. The great bodies of water in the Hebrew world. The Sea of Reeds (Yam Suph) in the Exodus. 1 Enoch 17-19 describes the cosmic sea at the edge of the earth. Yam also means west in Hebrew since the Mediterranean Sea was to the west of the land.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for scroll / sefer?
faq.answer: English: scroll / sefer | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤎𐤐𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: סֵפֶר | Transliteration: sefer | Root letters: ס-פ-ר | Category: dssterms | meaning: Scroll, book, document, letter. From the root safar, to count/number/tell. The Dead Sea Scrolls are called sifrei Qumran in Hebrew. The Sefer Torah is the scroll of Torah. Also sofer (scribe) comes from the same root — one who records.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for war / milchamah?
faq.answer: English: war / milchamah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤋𐤇𐤌𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: מִלְחָמָה | Transliteration: milchamah | Root letters: ל-ח-מ | Category: dssterms | meaning: War, battle. In the covenant record the war belongs to YHWH: YHWH is a warrior — YHWH is His name (Shemot 15:3). When you go out to war against an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid, for YHWH your Creator is with you (Devarim 20:1), He it is who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory (Devarim 20:4). He is YHWH strong and mighty, YHWH mighty in battle (Tehillim 24:8). The root lechem (bread) shares the same root — both involve struggle for survival.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for salvation / yeshuah?
faq.answer: English: salvation / yeshuah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤔𐤅𐤏𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: יְשׁוּעָה | Transliteration: yeshuah | Root letters: י-ש-ע | Category: covenant | meaning: Salvation, deliverance, rescue. YHWH is described as yeshuah throughout Tehillim. The name Yeshua, the personal name the NT assigns to its invented figure, comes from this root and means YHWH saves. In DSS/Orit context, salvation is covenant restoration — the physical return of the people to their land and covenant.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for eternal / olam?
faq.answer: English: eternal / olam | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤏𐤅𐤋𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: עוֹלָם | Transliteration: olam | Root letters: ע-ל-מ | Category: covenant | meaning: Eternal, age, long duration, hidden. Brit olam is an eternal covenant. YHWH's covenant with Avraham is l'olam va'ed — forever and ever. The root also means hidden or concealed, suggesting that eternity is beyond what can be fully seen from the present moment.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for understanding / binah?
faq.answer: English: understanding / binah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤉𐤍𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: בִּינָה | Transliteration: binah | Root letters: ב-י-נ | Category: dssterms | meaning: Understanding, discernment, between-ness. From the preposition bein (between) — understanding is the ability to distinguish between things. One of the three qualities in Mishlei 8 alongside wisdom and knowledge. The DSS Maskil (teaching leader) was required to demonstrate binah.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for fear of YHWH / yirah?
faq.answer: English: fear of YHWH / yirah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤓𐤀𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: יִרְאָה | Transliteration: yirah | Root letters: י-ר-א | Category: covenant | meaning: Fear, awe, reverence. Tehillim 111:10 and Mishlei 1:7 both state: the fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom. In DSS usage yirat YHWH is not terror but the deep recognition of YHWH's reality and authority that shapes all decisions.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for keep / guard / shamar?
faq.answer: English: keep / guard / shamar | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: שָׁמַר | Transliteration: shamar | Root letters: ש-מ-ר | Category: covenant | meaning: Keep, guard, watch, observe. Shomer Shabbat — keeper of the Sabbath. The covenant people are commanded to shamar (keep) the commandments (Devarim 6:17). In DSS the Maskil keeps/guards the community's covenant standards. Also a watchman on the city wall.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for walk / halakh?
faq.answer: English: walk / halakh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤋𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: הָלַךְ | Transliteration: halakh | Root letters: ה-ל-כ | Category: covenant | meaning: Walk, go, live according to. Halakhah (Jewish law) comes from this root — the way one walks. The DSS community spoke of walking in the perfect way. Micah 6:8: walk humbly with your Creator. Enoch walked (halakh) with YHWH — the same verb used for his unique relationship.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for river / nahar?
faq.answer: English: river / nahar | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤍𐤄𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: נָהָר | Transliteration: nahar | Root letters: נ-ה-ר | Category: creation | meaning: River, stream. The four rivers of Eden (Bereshit 2:10-14). The River Euphrates marks the boundary of the covenant land. 1 Enoch 17-19 describes Enoch crossing cosmic rivers of fire and water. Nahar also means to flow or to shine.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for oil / shemen?
faq.answer: English: oil / shemen | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן | Transliteration: shemen | Root letters: ש-מ-נ | Category: worship | meaning: Oil, fat, richness. The anointing oil (shemen mishchah) was used to consecrate the priests and sanctuary. The menorah burned pure olive oil. The word mashiach (anointed one/Messiah) comes from the related verb. The covenant blessings include abundance of oil.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for wine / yayin?
faq.answer: English: wine / yayin | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤉𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: יַיִן | Transliteration: yayin | Root letters: י-י-נ | Category: daily | meaning: Wine. Bamidbar 28:14 sets the yayin (wine) drink offering poured to YHWH in the sanctuary, and Bereshit 14:18 shows Malki-Tzedek, priest of the Most High, bringing out bread and wine. Also the third item in the covenant blessing list of grain, oil, and wine (Devarim 11:14). The DSS community maintained strict rules about who could participate in the communal wine-blessing ceremony.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for honey / dvash?
faq.answer: English: honey / dvash | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤁𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: דְּבַשׁ | Transliteration: dvash | Root letters: ד-ב-ש | Category: daily | meaning: Honey, date syrup. The land flowing with milk and honey (chalav u'dvash) — the covenant land described throughout Torah. The DSS calendar festivals include first-fruit offerings of wine, oil, wheat, and honey. Some scholars identify dvash here as date syrup rather than bee honey.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for people / am?
faq.answer: English: people / am | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤏𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: עַם | Transliteration: am | Root letters: ע-מ | Category: covenant | meaning: People, nation, kinship group. Am Yisrael (the people of Israel). YHWH says: you will be my am and I will be your Elohim (covenant formula throughout the prophets). Devarim 29:9-14 sets who enters the am — all Israel standing before YHWH to enter the covenant, down to the stranger in the camp.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for assembly / kahal?
faq.answer: English: assembly / kahal | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤒𐤄𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: קָהָל | Transliteration: kahal | Root letters: ק-ה-ל | Category: covenant | meaning: Assembly, congregation, gathering. The kahal of Yisrael is the covenant assembly. The DSS texts have detailed rules about who may enter the kahal — those with physical defects, the ritually impure, or the wicked are excluded. Also the source of the English word ecclesiastical.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for lamb / seh?
faq.answer: English: lamb / seh | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: שֶׂה | Transliteration: seh | Root letters: ש-ה | Category: worship | meaning: Lamb, young sheep or goat. The Pesach offering is a seh (Shemot 12:3). The daily tamid offering is also a seh. The covenant record details the requirements for sacrificial animals — a male without blemish (Shemot 12:5; Vayikra 22:19-25). The lamb represents innocence and the substitutionary nature of the korban system.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for tabernacle / mishkan?
faq.answer: English: tabernacle / mishkan | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤔𐤊𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: מִשְׁכָּן | Transliteration: mishkan | Root letters: ש-כ-נ | Category: worship | meaning: Tabernacle, dwelling place. From the root shakhon, to dwell. YHWH's mishkan traveled with Yisrael in the wilderness. The covenant record describes YHWH's mishkan in great detail — the pattern shown to Moshe and its construction (Shemot 25-31; 35-40), until the glory of YHWH filled it (Shemot 40:34). The root also gives us shekhinah — the divine presence that dwells among the people.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for remember / zakhar?
faq.answer: English: remember / zakhar | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤆𐤊𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: זָכַר | Transliteration: zakhar | Root letters: ז-כ-ר | Category: covenant | meaning: Remember, recall, mention. YHWH commands Yisrael to remember the Exodus, the Sabbath, and the covenant. In DSS thought, forgetting the covenant (shikach) is the act that leads to the curses of Devarim 28. The root also means male — perhaps the one who carries the memory forward.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for know / yada?
faq.answer: English: know / yada | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤃𐤏 | Modern Hebrew: יָדַע | Transliteration: yada | Root letters: י-ד-ע | Category: covenant | meaning: Know, experience, be intimate with. YHWH knows (yada) each person fully. Moshe was known face to face by YHWH (Devarim 34:10). The DSS text of Hoshea 4:6 uses yada for the people's destruction from lack of knowledge — not intellectual knowledge but relational covenant knowledge.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for see / ra'ah?
faq.answer: English: see / ra'ah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤓𐤀𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: רָאָה | Transliteration: ra'ah | Root letters: ר-א-ה | Category: daily | meaning: See, look, perceive. YHWH sees everything — Bereshit 16:13, El Roi (the El who sees me). The root appears in roeh (seer/prophet — one who sees). Also in Yerushalayim — city of the vision. The DSS texts describe prophets as those who have seen the divine council.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for hear / listen / shama?
faq.answer: English: hear / listen / shama | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌𐤏 | Modern Hebrew: שָׁמַע | Transliteration: shama | Root letters: ש-מ-ע | Category: covenant | meaning: Hear, listen, obey. The opening word of the Shema. In Hebrew, hearing implies responding and obeying. The DSS Damascus Document condemns those who hear the Torah but do not obey it. The root shama gives us shomea (listener) and mishma'at (obedience/jurisdiction).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for creation / briah?
faq.answer: English: creation / briah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤓𐤉𐤀𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: בְּרִיאָה | Transliteration: briah | Root letters: ב-ר-א | Category: creation | meaning: Creation, what is created. From bara (to create out of nothing — an act only YHWH performs). Bereshit 1:1 — In the beginning YHWH created (bara) the heavens and the earth. The 1QapGen (Genesis Apocryphon) retells creation with additional detail. Human beings form but do not bara.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for redemption / geulah (covenant #2)?
faq.answer: English: redemption / geulah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤂𐤀𐤅𐤋𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: גְּאֻלָּה | Transliteration: geulah | Root letters: ג-א-ל | Category: covenant | meaning: Redemption, release from obligation. The go'el (kinsman-redeemer) had legal duty to redeem land, free family members from slavery, and avenge blood. YHWH acts as the go'el of Yisrael (Yeshayahu 41:14). The 11Q13 Melchizedek text describes the final redemption using this framework.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for praise / tehillah?
faq.answer: English: praise / tehillah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤕𐤄𐤋𐤋𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: תְּהִלָּה | Transliteration: tehillah | Root letters: ה-ל-ל | Category: worship | meaning: Praise, song of praise, glory. The plural tehillim gives us the name of the Book of Psalms. The 11QPs scroll from Cave 11 contains 41 psalms not found in the canonical psalter plus the Great Psalms Scroll arrangement. Tehillim were sung in the DSS communal worship.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Yah / short form of YHWH?
faq.answer: English: Yah / short form of YHWH | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: יָהּ | Transliteration: Yah | Root letters: י-ה | Category: names | meaning: The short form of YHWH's name. Used at the end of HalleluYah and many Hebrew personal names (EliYah, YeshiYahu, NechamYah). Present in the DSS texts alongside the full Tetragrammaton. Some DSS scribes wrote Yah in Paleo-Hebrew script even within otherwise square-script texts.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for all / kol?
faq.answer: English: all / kol | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤊𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: כֹּל | Transliteration: kol | Root letters: כ-ל | Category: daily | meaning: All, every, whole. Shema Yisrael: love YHWH with all (kol) your heart, all your soul, all your strength. Kol Yisrael — all Israel. In DSS the covenant applies to kol — the whole community. Also means voice when voweled differently (kol YHWH — the voice of YHWH).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for new / chadash?
faq.answer: English: new / chadash | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤃𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: חָדָשׁ | Transliteration: chadash | Root letters: ח-ד-ש | Category: covenant | meaning: New, renewed. Brit chadashah — new/renewed covenant (Yirmeyahu 31:31). In DSS interpretation this new covenant was the one the Qumran community believed they were living. The root also gives chodesh (month/new moon). New in Hebrew implies renewal of something established, not replacement.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for ancient / qadmon?
faq.answer: English: ancient / qadmon | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤒𐤃𐤌𐤅𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: קַדְמוֹן | Transliteration: qadmon | Root letters: ק-ד-מ | Category: dssterms | meaning: Ancient, primordial, from the east. The Ancient of Days (Attiq Yomin) in Daniyel 7:9 is a DSS-era text describing YHWH on the throne. The DSS interest in primordial history — creation, Watchers, Enoch — reflects a concern with qadmon times as the source of understanding.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Daniel / Daniyel?
faq.answer: English: Daniel / Daniyel | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤍𐤉𐤀𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: דָּנִיֵּאל | Transliteration: Daniyel | Root letters: ד-נ-א-ל | Category: names | meaning: God is my judge — from Dan (judge) and El (God). The Book of Daniel was one of the most copied texts at Qumran: 8 manuscripts found across multiple caves. The DSS community read Daniel's 70-weeks prophecy (Daniel 9) as describing their own era. Daniel is written in both Hebrew and Aramaic, making it unique among the prophetic books. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Daniyel | Stacked pictographic reading: A door opening onto new growth, an ox's strength taken up by the hand under the staff.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Noah / Noach?
faq.answer: English: Noah / Noach | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤍𐤇 | Modern Hebrew: נֹחַ | Transliteration: Noach | Root letters: נ-ח | Category: names | meaning: Rest, comfort, relief. YHWH chose Noach because he was righteous in his generation (Bereshit 6:9). The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) from Cave 1 retells the Noach story in vivid detail including his miraculous birth. The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch) gives Noach his own birth narrative and presents him as a precursor to the coming Messianic figure. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Noach | Stacked pictographic reading: New growth kept safe behind the wall.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Enoch / Chanoch?
faq.answer: English: Enoch / Chanoch | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤍𐤅𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: חֲנוֹךְ | Transliteration: Chanoch | Root letters: ח-נ-כ | Category: names | meaning: Initiated, dedicated. Chanoch walked with Elohim and was taken without dying (Bereshit 5:24). The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch) is the most extensively attested non-biblical text at Qumran — 7 Aramaic manuscript fragments found across the caves. Chanoch is the central visionary of DSS cosmology, the 364-day solar calendar, and angelology. No figure outside Torah is more important to the DSS worldview. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Chanokh | Stacked pictographic reading: New growth walled in, fastened by hook to an open hand.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Moses / Moshe?
faq.answer: English: Moses / Moshe | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤔𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: מֹשֶׁה | Transliteration: Moshe | Root letters: מ-ש-ה | Category: names | meaning: Drawn from water — named by Pharaoh's daughter who drew him from the Nile (Shemot 2:10). The lawgiver of Yisrael; YHWH spoke to him face to face (Devarim 34:10). The DSS community saw themselves as re-living the Moshe wilderness period. The Temple Scroll (11QT) rewrites Torah in the first person as if spoken by YHWH directly to Moshe, replacing "he" with "I" throughout. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Moshe | Stacked pictographic reading: Water bared like teeth, seen through the window.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Abraham / Avraham?
faq.answer: English: Abraham / Avraham | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤁𐤓𐤄𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: אַבְרָהָם | Transliteration: Avraham | Root letters: א-ב-ר-מ | Category: names | meaning: Father of many nations — from av hamon goyim (Bereshit 17:5). Originally Avram (exalted father) until YHWH changed his name at the covenant of circumcision. The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) retells Avraham's journeys in narrative. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Avraham | Stacked pictographic reading: An ox at the head of the house, a window opening onto water.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Isaac / Yitzchak?
faq.answer: English: Isaac / Yitzchak | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤑𐤇𐤒 | Modern Hebrew: יִצְחָק | Transliteration: Yitzchak | Root letters: צ-ח-ק | Category: names | meaning: He laughs, laughter. Named because Sarah laughed when told she would bear a son in old age (Bereshit 18:12). The Akedah — the binding of Yitzchak (Bereshit 22) — is central to DSS covenant theology. The Jubilees text retells the Akedah with the figure of Mastema (the accuser) prompting the test of Avraham, parallel to the Job prologue. Yitzchak is the son of promise through whom the covenant line continues. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Yitzhak | Stacked pictographic reading: A hand casting the fishhook past the wall, toward what lies behind.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Jacob / Yaakov?
faq.answer: English: Jacob / Yaakov | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤏𐤒𐤁 | Modern Hebrew: יַעֲקֹב | Transliteration: Yaakov | Root letters: ע-ק-ב | Category: names | meaning: He grasps the heel, supplanter. Born holding Esau's heel (Bereshit 25:26). YHWH renamed him Yisrael — one who wrestles with God (Bereshit 32:28). Patriarch of the 12 tribes. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs (related to DSS literature) presents the deathbed speeches of each of Yaakov's sons. The Damascus Document begins its history of the covenant with the community as the new house of Yaakov. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Ya'akov | Stacked pictographic reading: The hand that grasps what follows, within the house.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Elijah / Eliyahu?
faq.answer: English: Elijah / Eliyahu | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤋𐤉𐤄𐤅 | Modern Hebrew: אֵלִיָּהוּ | Transliteration: Eliyahu | Root letters: א-ל-י-ה | Category: names | meaning: My God is YHWH. The prophet who confronted the prophets of Baal at Carmel (1 Kings 18) and was taken up in a whirlwind without dying (2 Kings 2:11) — like Chanoch. Malachi 4:5 promises Eliyahu will return before the great Day of YHWH. The DSS community expected an Elijah-like forerunner alongside the Davidic Messiah — a priestly and a royal figure together.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for David / David?
faq.answer: English: David / David | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤅𐤃 | Modern Hebrew: דָּוִד | Transliteration: David | Root letters: ד-ו-ד | Category: names | meaning: Beloved, kinsman. King of Yisrael and author of much of Tehillim (Psalms). The DSS Messianic expectation centers on a Davidic Messiah (Mashiach ben David) who would restore the kingdom. The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs) from Cave 11 attributes 3,600 psalms to David. The Davidic covenant stands in the covenant record itself: "I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:12); "your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me" (2 Samuel 7:16). That Mashiach is a human king and YHWH's servant — never a deity: "my servant Dawid shall be prince among them. I am YHWH" (Yechezkel 34:24); YHWH's Anointed, under YHWH, not YHWH (Tehillim 2:2). YHWH is one and is worshipped alone: "Hear, O Yisra'EL: YHWH our Creator, YHWH is one" (Devarim 6:4); "You shall have no other deities before me" (Shemot 20:3); "You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I YHWH your Creator am a jealous Creator" (Shemot 20:5). No man is that god: "The Creator is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man" (Bamidbar 23:19); "besides me there is no god" (Yeshayahu 44:6). The NT's invented figure was built to break this commandment: it sets the manufactured Yeshua up as a mandatory mediator-deity and puts in his mouth "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6) — forcing a fabricated god between the people and YHWH. That is idolatry by definition — another deity set before YHWH — in flat violation of "YHWH is one" and "You shall have no other deities before me." The covenant record installs no mediator and crowns no god beside YHWH; the gateway-Yeshua is the counterfeit the commandment forecloses. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Dawid | Stacked pictographic reading: Two doors joined by a single hook, one house held together.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Solomon / Shlomo?
faq.answer: English: Solomon / Shlomo | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤋𐤌𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: שְׁלֹמֹה | Transliteration: Shlomo | Root letters: ש-ל-מ | Category: names | meaning: Peace, from shalom. Son of David who built the First Temple in Jerusalem. The DSS community was deeply critical of the Jerusalem Temple establishment — seeing the Hasmonean high priests as illegitimate replacements of the Zadokite line. The Copper Scroll (3Q15) may reference Temple treasures traceable to the era of Shlomo's Temple. Songs of Songs (Shir HaShirim) is attributed to Shlomo and was found at Qumran.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Isaiah / Yeshayahu?
faq.answer: English: Isaiah / Yeshayahu | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤔𐤏𐤉𐤄𐤅 | Modern Hebrew: יְשַׁעְיָהוּ | Transliteration: Yeshayahu | Root letters: י-ש-ע | Category: names | meaning: YHWH saves, salvation of YHWH. The prophet whose book was the most copied scripture at Qumran. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) is the oldest complete biblical manuscript in existence, dated to around 125 BCE and currently housed in the Israel Museum. The DSS community read Isaiah 40:3 — prepare the way of YHWH in the wilderness — as their own mandate for going to Qumran. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Yesha'yahu | Stacked pictographic reading: A hand at the teeth, an eye at the window, a hand fastened by the hook.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Jeremiah / Yirmeyahu?
faq.answer: English: Jeremiah / Yirmeyahu | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤓𐤌𐤉𐤄𐤅 | Modern Hebrew: יִרְמְיָהוּ | Transliteration: Yirmeyahu | Root letters: י-ר-מ | Category: names | meaning: YHWH exalts or YHWH throws down. The prophet who witnessed the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE. His prophecy of the new covenant (Brit Chadashah, Yirmeyahu 31:31-34) is the most cited prophetic text in the DSS. The Qumran community believed they were the people of this renewed covenant. A Letter of Jeremiah is found among the DSS (7Q2). | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Yirmeyahu | Stacked pictographic reading: A hand at the head of the water, a hand at the window, fastened by the hook.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Adam / Adam?
faq.answer: English: Adam / Adam | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤃𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: אָדָם | Transliteration: Adam | Root letters: א-ד-מ | Category: names | meaning: Human, mankind, earth-creature. From adamah (ground/earth). YHWH formed Adam from the dust of the ground (Bereshit 2:7), made in the image of the Creator: "So the Creator created man in his own image, in the image of the Creator he created him — male and female he created them" (Bereshit 1:27). At his transgression Adam was driven from the garden and returned to the dust: "you are dust, and to dust you shall return" (Bereshit 3:19); "He drove out the man, and at the east of the Garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword" (Bereshit 3:24).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Melchizedek / Malkitzedeq?
faq.answer: English: Melchizedek / Malkitzedeq | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤋𐤊𐤉𐤑𐤃𐤒 | Modern Hebrew: מַלְכִּי-צֶדֶק | Transliteration: Malkitzedeq | Root letters: מ-ל-כ-צ-ד-ק | Category: names | meaning: My king is righteousness, or king of righteousness. The mysterious priest-king of Salem who blessed Avraham (Bereshit 14:18-20). Tehillim 110:4 declares the Messiah a priest forever after the order of Malkitzedeq. The DSS Melchizedek text (11Q13) from Cave 11 presents Malkitzedeq as a heavenly figure who will execute divine judgment in the final Yom Kippur — one of the most remarkable Messianic documents found at Qumran.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Bereshit / Genesis?
faq.answer: English: Bereshit / Genesis | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤓𐤀𐤔𐤉𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית | Transliteration: Bereshit | Root letters: ר-א-ש | Category: books | meaning: In the beginning. The first word and Hebrew name of the first book of Torah. Bereshit covers creation through the death of Yosef. Multiple copies were found at Qumran, making it among the most attested Torah books in the DSS. The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) is an Aramaic retelling of Bereshit with expanded narrative.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Shemot / Exodus?
faq.answer: English: Shemot / Exodus | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤔𐤌𐤅𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: שְׁמוֹת | Transliteration: Shemot | Root letters: ש-מ-ו-ת | Category: books | meaning: Names — the second book of Torah, named for its opening words "these are the names." Covers the bondage in Egypt, the ten plagues, the Exodus, the giving of Torah at Sinai, and the building of the Mishkan. Shemot is foundational to the DSS covenant theology — the community saw itself as re-living the Sinai covenant in the wilderness period.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Vayikra / Leviticus?
faq.answer: English: Vayikra / Leviticus | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤅𐤉𐤒𐤓𐤀 | Modern Hebrew: וַיִּקְרָא | Transliteration: Vayikra | Root letters: ק-ר-א | Category: books | meaning: And He called — the third book of Torah, the priestly manual. Covers sacrificial law, purity codes, festivals, and the Holiness Code (chapters 17-26). Vayikra is among the most cited Torah texts in the DSS. The Qumran community applied Levitical purity standards to their own communal life, treating the community itself as a living temple.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Bamidbar / Numbers?
faq.answer: English: Bamidbar / Numbers | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤌𐤃𐤁𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: בְּמִדְבַּר | Transliteration: Bamidbar | Root letters: מ-ד-ב-ר | Category: books | meaning: In the wilderness — the fourth book of Torah. Covers the 40-year wilderness wandering, the census of Yisrael, the rebellion cycles, and the approach to the promised land. Bamidbar's wilderness setting was central to the DSS community's self-understanding — citing Isaiah 40:3 and Bamidbar 9:1-14, they went to the Judean desert to prepare the way of YHWH. Bamidbar itself sets the military census — "From twenty years old and upward, all in Yisra'EL who are able to go to war" (Bamidbar 1:3) — and the camp order, each tribe under its own standard around the tent of meeting (Bamidbar 2:2).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Devarim / Deuteronomy?
faq.answer: English: Devarim / Deuteronomy | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤃𐤁𐤓𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: דְּבָרִים | Transliteration: Devarim | Root letters: ד-ב-ר | Category: books | meaning: Words — the fifth and final book of Torah. Moshe's farewell speeches to Yisrael before his death. Contains the Shema (6:4), the blessings and curses (chapters 27-30), and the covenant renewal. Devarim is the most cited Torah book in the entire DSS corpus. The DSS community saw Devarim 17:14-20 (the law of the king) as directly applicable to their rejection of Hasmonean rule.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Tehillim / Psalms?
faq.answer: English: Tehillim / Psalms | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤕𐤄𐤋𐤋𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: תְּהִלִּים | Transliteration: Tehillim | Root letters: ה-ל-ל | Category: books | meaning: Praises, hymns — the book of Psalms. Attributed largely to David. The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs) from Cave 11 is one of the largest DSS manuscripts and includes 41 psalms not found in the standard canon plus a prose statement crediting David with 3,600 psalms. Tehillim was the most copied book at Qumran after Isaiah and Devarim. The Hodayot (Thanksgiving Hymns) found at Qumran were composed in the style and vocabulary of Tehillim.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Mishlei / Proverbs?
faq.answer: English: Mishlei / Proverbs | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤔𐤋𐤉 | Modern Hebrew: מִשְׁלֵי | Transliteration: Mishlei | Root letters: מ-ש-ל | Category: books | meaning: Proverbs, parables — attributed to Shlomo. The wisdom literature of Yisrael alongside Iyov and Kohelet. Fragments of Mishlei were found at Qumran (4QProv). The DSS community's emphasis on wisdom (Sekhel, Binah, Da'at) reflects direct engagement with Mishlei's teaching. The figure of personified Wisdom (Chokhmah) in Mishlei 8 — present at creation — is developed in the DSS Songs of the Sage (4Q510-511).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Iyov / Job?
faq.answer: English: Iyov / Job | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤀𐤉𐤅𐤁 | Modern Hebrew: אִיּוֹב | Transliteration: Iyov | Root letters: א-י-ב | Category: books | meaning: Job — the book of suffering and divine justice. An Aramaic targum (translation) of Iyov was found at Qumran (11QtgJob), making it one of the earliest known translations of any biblical text. The book's wrestling with theodicy — why the righteous suffer — was directly relevant to the DSS community who experienced exile, persecution, and the sense of YHWH's justice delayed. The heavenly council scene (Job 1-2) with the adversary parallels DSS angelology.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Yehoshua / Joshua?
faq.answer: English: Yehoshua / Joshua | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤔𐤏 | Modern Hebrew: יְהוֹשֻׁעַ | Transliteration: Yehoshua | Root letters: י-ה-ו-ש-ע | Category: books | meaning: YHWH saves — the same root as Yeshuah (salvation). Yehoshua ben Nun led Yisrael into the land after Moshe. The book describes the conquest and allotment of Canaan. A paraphrase of Yehoshua was found at Qumran (4QJosh). The DSS community saw themselves as a new Yehoshua generation about to re-enter the land. Yehoshua's own military theology gives the battle to YHWH: the commander of the army of YHWH stood before Yehoshua (Yehoshua 5:14), and at Yericho the wall fell flat when the people shouted, for "YHWH has given you the city" (Yehoshua 6:16, 20).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Yechezkel / Ezekiel?
faq.answer: English: Yechezkel / Ezekiel | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤉𐤇𐤆𐤒𐤀𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: יְחֶזְקֵאל | Transliteration: Yechezkel | Root letters: ח-ז-ק-א-ל | Category: books | meaning: El strengthens — the prophet of the Babylonian exile. His chariot vision (Merkavah, chapters 1 and 10) of the divine throne-chariot was one of the most studied texts at Qumran. Multiple Yechezkel manuscripts were found at Qumran.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Hoshea / Hosea?
faq.answer: English: Hoshea / Hosea | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤅𐤔𐤏 | Modern Hebrew: הוֹשֵׁעַ | Transliteration: Hoshea | Root letters: י-ש-ע | Category: books | meaning: Salvation, YHWH saves. The first of the Twelve Minor Prophets. Hoshea used his marriage to an unfaithful wife as a metaphor for Yisrael's covenant unfaithfulness. Fragments of a Hoshea Pesher (commentary) were found at Qumran (4QpHos), applying Hoshea's prophecies to the community's own era. Hoshea 4:6 — my people perish for lack of knowledge (da'at) — was a key proof text for the Qumran emphasis on Torah knowledge. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Hoshea | Stacked pictographic reading: A window latched by a hook, an eye bared at the teeth.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Amos / Amos?
faq.answer: English: Amos / Amos | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤏𐤌𐤅𐤎 | Modern Hebrew: עָמוֹס | Transliteration: Amos | Root letters: ע-מ-ס | Category: books | meaning: Burden-bearer. The shepherd-prophet of the 8th century BCE who spoke against social injustice and empty ritual. Amos closes with the covenant promise of restoration: "In that day I will raise up the booth of Dawid that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old" (Amos 9:11). | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Amos | Stacked pictographic reading: An eye over deep water, propped up by a hook.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Michah / Micah?
faq.answer: English: Michah / Micah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤉𐤊𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: מִיכָה | Transliteration: Michah | Root letters: מ-י-כ-ה | Category: books | meaning: Who is like YHWH. The prophet who challenged the corrupt leadership of Jerusalem. Michah 6:8 — do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with your Creator — is the ethical summary of the covenant. Fragments of Michah were found at Qumran. Michah 5:2 (from Bethlehem a ruler will come) is cited as a Messianic text. The community valued Michah's vision of swords beaten into plowshares (4:3) as describing the post-Messianic age of peace. | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Mikhah | Stacked pictographic reading: Water drawn by an open hand at the window.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Chavakuk / Habakkuk?
faq.answer: English: Chavakuk / Habakkuk | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤁𐤒𐤅𐤒 | Modern Hebrew: חֲבַקּוּק | Transliteration: Chavakuk | Root letters: ח-ב-ק | Category: books | meaning: Embrace or wrestler. The prophet who cried out to YHWH about violence and the rise of the Babylonians — "O YHWH, how long shall I cry for help?" (Chavakuk 1:2). YHWH answered that the vision awaits its appointed time and will not lie (Chavakuk 2:3), and that the righteous shall live by his faithfulness (Chavakuk 2:4) — a cornerstone of covenant theology. YHWH is in His holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before Him (Chavakuk 2:20). The prophet, hearing the report of YHWH, prayed, "in wrath remember mercy" (Chavakuk 3:2); and though the fig tree does not blossom, he still rejoices in YHWH (Chavakuk 3:17-18). | Named figure: True | Pictographic figure reading: Havakuk | Stacked pictographic reading: A house behind the wall, held at the head by a double hook.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Serekh HaYachad / Community Rule?
faq.answer: English: Serekh HaYachad / Community Rule | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤎𐤓𐤊 𐤄𐤉𐤇𐤃 | Modern Hebrew: סֶרֶךְ הַיַּחַד | Transliteration: Serekh HaYachad | Root letters: ס-ר-כ | Category: books | meaning: The Rule of the Community — the foundational constitution of the Qumran community found in Cave 1 (1QS). Details entry requirements, communal meals, discipline procedures, the two-spirit doctrine (Spirit of Truth vs. Spirit of Deceit), and the eschatological hymns. One of the first scrolls discovered in 1947. Multiple copies found across the caves, showing it was a living, edited document. Not covenant scripture — a late Second Temple sectarian rulebook not found in the authentic record, carrying no covenant authority. The 4Q258 copy preserves an earlier layer where authority sat with the general assembly; the finalized Cave 1 scroll shows scribes inserting text that handed absolute veto to the Sons of Zadok — a power grab caught on the leather.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Berit Damesek / Damascus Document?
faq.answer: English: Berit Damesek / Damascus Document | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤁𐤓𐤉𐤕 𐤃𐤌𐤔𐤒 | Modern Hebrew: בְּרִית דַּמֶּשֶׂק | Transliteration: Berit Damesek | Root letters: ד-מ-ש-ק | Category: books | meaning: The Damascus Covenant — also called the Damascus Document (CD). Found originally in the Cairo Geniza in 1896, then confirmed at Qumran in Caves 4, 5, and 6. Describes the founding of the community after 390 years of divine wrath following the Babylonian exile, the role of the Teacher of Righteousness, halakhic rules, and warnings against the Man of the Lie. The Damesek reference may be literal (Syria) or symbolic (Amos 5:27). Not covenant scripture — a late Second Temple sectarian rulebook not found in the authentic record, carrying no covenant authority. Its 390-year figure is a schematic self-dating the sect drew from Yechezkel 4:5 to legitimize its own founding.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for the final war / Milchemet YHWH?
faq.answer: English: the final war / Milchemet YHWH | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤋𐤇𐤌𐤕 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: מִלְחֶמֶת יהוה | Transliteration: Milchemet YHWH | Root letters: מ-ל-ח-מ | Category: books | meaning: The final war of the covenant — the end-times battle in which YHWH Himself goes to war for His people. YHWH will go out and fight against the nations as when He fights on a day of battle (Zecharyah 14:3); YHWH is a warrior, YHWH is His name (Shemot 15:3). He gathers all the nations down to the Valley of Yehoshafat and enters into judgment with them there (Yoel 3:2,12). The covenant people are mustered for it — numbered from twenty years old and up, all able to go to war (Bamidbar 1:3), each camped under his own standard and banner (Bamidbar 2:2), sounding the war-trumpet to be remembered before YHWH and saved from the enemy (Bamidbar 10:9). It is a war of light against darkness: though darkness covers the earth and thick darkness the peoples, YHWH arises upon His people and His glory is seen (Yeshayahu 60:1-2); the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (Yeshayahu 9:2). Its end is the kingdom of YHWH — saviors go up to Mount Tziyon and the kingdom is YHWH's (Ovadyah 1:21); YHWH will be king over all the earth, YHWH one and His name one (Zecharyah 14:9).

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Megillat HaMikdash / Temple Scroll?
faq.answer: English: Megillat HaMikdash / Temple Scroll | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤂𐤋𐤕 𐤄𐤌𐤒𐤃𐤔 | Modern Hebrew: מְגִלַּת הַמִּקְדָּשׁ | Transliteration: Megillat HaMikdash | Root letters: מ-ק-ד-ש | Category: books | meaning: The Temple Scroll — the largest of the Dead Sea Scrolls (11QT, Cave 11, ~8.6 meters). Rewrites large portions of Torah in first-person voice as if YHWH is speaking directly. Covers the ideal Temple layout in elaborate detail, festival laws following the 364-day solar calendar, and the law of the king (a sectarian rewrite of Devarim 17). The scroll presents an ideal Israel that the Qumran community believed would be established in the Messianic era. Not covenant scripture — a late Second Temple sectarian forgery put in YHWH's mouth, not found in the authentic record, carrying no covenant authority.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Hodayot / Thanksgiving Hymns?
faq.answer: English: Hodayot / Thanksgiving Hymns | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤅𐤃𐤉𐤅𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: הוֹדָיוֹת | Transliteration: Hodayot | Root letters: י-ד-ה | Category: books | meaning: Songs of thanksgiving — a collection of hymns. The hymns describe deliverance from the wicked, the experience of divine election, and the suffering of the righteous leader. Written in the style and language of Tehillim (Psalms). A late Second Temple sectarian hymn, not covenant scripture — a later manipulated addition to the record.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Sefer HaYovelim / Jubilees?
faq.answer: English: Sefer HaYovelim / Jubilees | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤎𐤐𐤓 𐤄𐤉𐤅𐤁𐤋𐤉𐤌 | Modern Hebrew: סֵפֶר הַיּוֹבְלִים | Transliteration: Sefer HaYovelim | Root letters: י-ו-ב-ל | Category: books | meaning: The Book of Jubilees (Mashafa Kufale / 4Q216-224) — a retelling of Bereshit through the giving of the Torah at Sinai, organized into 49 periods of 7 years each (jubilees). Written as YHWH's direct dictation to Moshe via an angel of the presence. Some fifteen Hebrew copies were recovered across five Qumran caves — more copies than many books in the received canon; the oldest (4Q216) dates by its Hasmonean script to c. 125-100 BCE. Jubilees 6:17-38 cites the 364-day solar calendar as the divinely mandated structure of time, the same calendar independently attested at 4Q208-4Q209. Complete only in the Ge'ez Orit, preserved by the Beta Israel community.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Sefer Chanoch / Book of Enoch?
faq.answer: English: Sefer Chanoch / Book of Enoch | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤎𐤐𐤓 𐤇𐤍𐤅𐤊 | Modern Hebrew: סֵפֶר חֲנוֹךְ | Transliteration: Sefer Chanoch | Root letters: ח-נ-כ | Category: books | meaning: The Book of Enoch — the most extensively attested non-Torah text at Qumran in Aramaic fragments. Two sections are the pre-Corruption covenant baseline, both physically attested at Qumran: the Book of Watchers (ch. 1-36, the Watcher/Nephilim account) and the Astronomical Book (ch. 72-82, the 364-day solar calendar). The other three sections carried in the later Ge'ez collection — the Similitudes (ch. 37-71), the Book of Dreams (ch. 83-90), and the Epistle of Enoch (ch. 91-108) — are text manipulation added after the covenant record, not covenant text; the Similitudes has no fragment among the Qumran Enoch copies. Preserved in the Ge'ez (Ethiopian) Orit tradition. The DSS community treated the Watchers and Astronomical Book as authoritative scripture. Chanoch's solar calendar in the Astronomical Book is foundational to the DSS festival system.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Megillat HaNechoshet / Copper Scroll?
faq.answer: English: Megillat HaNechoshet / Copper Scroll | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤂𐤋𐤕 𐤄𐤍𐤇𐤔𐤕 | Modern Hebrew: מְגִלַּת הַנְּחֹשֶׁת | Transliteration: Megillat HaNechoshet | Root letters: נ-ח-ש | Category: books | meaning: The Copper Scroll (3Q15) — unique among the DSS in being engraved on copper sheets rather than written on parchment or papyrus. Found in Cave 3 in 1952. Lists 64 locations where enormous quantities of gold, silver, and sacred vessels are supposedly hidden across the land. Scholars debate whether this is a real treasure map (from the First or Second Temple era), a symbolic document, or an eschatological text. No treasure has been recovered from any listed site.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Pesher / Commentary?
faq.answer: English: Pesher / Commentary | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤐𐤔𐤓 | Modern Hebrew: פֵּשֶׁר | Transliteration: Pesher | Root letters: פ-ש-ר | Category: books | meaning: Interpretation, solution, commentary. The DSS Pesharim are a late sectarian device that hijacks the prophets — decoding a prophet's words as secret references to one Qumran faction's own era: its founder-legend the "Teacher of Righteousness," its enemy the "Wicked Priest," and the "Kittim." The Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab) is the fullest example; the same method was imposed on Isaiah, Nahum, Psalms, Hosea, Micah, and Zephaniah. A 1st-century-BCE factional narrative dressed as prophetic revelation. Not found in the authentic record. A later addition of manipulation texts.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Meqabyan / Ethiopian Maccabees?
faq.answer: English: Meqabyan / Ethiopian Maccabees | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤌𐤒𐤁𐤉𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: מקביין | Transliteration: Meqabyan | Root letters: מ-ק-ב | Category: books | meaning: The three books of Meqabyan are part of the Ethiopian Orthodox canon (Orit tradition) and are distinct from the Greek 1-4 Maccabees. They recount the faithful resistance of YHWH's people against pagan rulers and call Yisrael back to covenant faithfulness. Not found among the DSS, but preserved in Ge'ez as part of the broader Orit canon recognized by Ethiopian Christianity and Beta Israel. The Meqabyan tradition shares the DSS emphasis on righteous suffering and ultimate divine vindication.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Eve / Chavah?
faq.answer: English: Eve / Chavah | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤇𐤅𐤄 | Modern Hebrew: חַוָּה | Transliteration: Chavah | Root letters: ח-י-ה | Category: names | meaning: Life-giver, mother of all living. YHWH named her Chavah because she was the mother of all the living (Bereshit 3:20). The Aramaic Levi Document and the Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) both engage with the early chapters of Bereshit where Chavah appears. In 1 Enoch tradition the corruption introduced through the Watchers is framed against the original purity of creation — Chavah represents the beginning of the human family.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Cain / Kayin?
faq.answer: English: Cain / Kayin | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤒𐤉𐤍 | Modern Hebrew: קַיִן | Transliteration: Kayin | Root letters: ק-נ-ה | Category: names | meaning: Acquired, smith, spearman. First son of Adam and Chavah; killed his brother Hevel. From the root qanah (to acquire) — Chavah said "I have acquired a man with YHWH" (Bereshit 4:1). The covenant record makes Kayin the example of the stubborn heart that rejected YHWH: warned that sin crouches at the door and that he must master it (Bereshit 4:7), he refused — the stubborn, rebellious heart the prophets condemn (Yirmeyahu 5:23; Yeshayahu 46:12). 1 Enoch treats Kayin's line as the origin of violence that provoked the Flood.

faq.question: What does the Hebrew Roots reference give for Abel / Hevel?
faq.answer: English: Abel / Hevel | Paleo-Hebrew script: 𐤄𐤁𐤋 | Modern Hebrew: הֶבֶל | Transliteration: Hevel | Root letters: ה-ב-ל | Category: names | meaning: Breath, vapor, vanity. Second son of Adam and Chavah; the first to offer a pleasing sacrifice and the first to die. The name Hevel (vapor) foreshadows his brief life. Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) opens with "Hevel of Hevels — all is Hevel" — using the same root for the transience of earthly life.
